  • It should come as little surprise that David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” focuses on, well, Cliff Booth.
  • Sources indicate that “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and, by extension, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” occupy a unique place in Tarantino’s cinematic world, as they’re both part of his so-called “Realer Than Real World Universe” and his “Movie Movie Universe.” Tarantino didn’t just keep crafting his movies-within-movies world with the hit film — he also introduced real-world (realer than real world?) elements and people (the Manson Family, of course, and all that entails).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

It should come as little surprise that David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” focuses on, well, Cliff Booth. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to the filmmaker’s own 2019 Oscar-winning hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” has always been billed as a spinoff following the continuing adventures of his fictitious (yet still iconic) stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). But Tarantino has always loved building out his own shared and connected universe(s), and fans sure love exploring its outer limits.

Sources indicate that “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and, by extension, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” occupy a unique place in Tarantino’s cinematic world, as they’re both part of his so-called “Realer Than Real World Universe” and his “Movie Movie Universe.” Tarantino didn’t just keep crafting his movies-within-movies world with the hit film — he also introduced real-world (realer than real world?) elements and people (the Manson Family, of course, and all that entails). Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

Sources indicate that that bent continues in “Cliff Booth,” which is rife with both out-there elements and very real references (time for that “Hee Haw” resurgence, we guess). But the film also has to follow its own series logic, which means, yes, it’s the Cliff Booth show, but hey, where are our “Hollywood” co-stars Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie)?

[Once again: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

According to recent reports, when we first meet Cliff and Rick, the duo are long-time colleagues and best pals. As his stunt double, Cliff is tasked with doing some serious heavy lifting for Hollywood star Rick, which inevitably (?) leads them to off four members of the Manson Family. The raucous and wild violence the duo inflicts on the foursome isn’t just a fun bonding exercise for the pair. It also ensures that the nefarious group can’t go next door to enact the infamous (and very real) Tate murders. Win-win!

It has been revealed that the film ends with an invitation for Rick to slide on over to the Tate house for a thank-you drink, presumably putting him in the path of Roman Polanski, Sharon, and all the star power they carry. “Cliff Booth” is set eight years after those events, and while Rick may have enjoyed a career upswing in the interim, his current professional endeavors have taken him far from Hollywood.

Industry observers note that while we never see Rick in the film (despite ongoing rumors that DiCaprio might appear for a quick cameo), Cliff mentions him frequently and fondly, including telling potential paramour Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) that their professional entanglements ended when Rick got, ahem, “too fat” for Cliff to believably double him and then moved to Australia to star in the TV series “Dingo Dan.” Further details on the show are slim, but we do know it’s a Western TV show that’s proven quite popular and durable (Aussie Karen seems to like it), and Cliff makes it sound like Rick is enjoying himself. Not too bad.

By blending his two movie universes with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Tarantino got to both delight in late-’60s Hollywood magic and “save” Sharon Tate, her unborn son, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski, Steven Parent, and Jay Sebring. That sort of revisionist history was the film’s buzziest twist and, as I argued at the time, the most emotional choice Tarantino has ever made in his filmography.

Sources indicate that and while we don’t get treated to much more Sharon in “Cliff Booth,” we are granted some, in the form of a Red Apple Cigarettes commercial led by a beaming Margot Robbie, returning to her original role as the doomed actress. (The fake cigarettes are another Tarantino-verse staple, and Rick even appears in his own commercial for them during the end credits of “Hollywood.”).

It has been revealed that in the short cameo, Sharon looks healthy and happy, and she’s clearly still enough of a star to warrant her own advertising campaign, built on her smile and her zippy shimmy. As Cliff watches the commercial at the Marina del Rey condo he shares with his dad (Peter Weller), he takes the time to stop, observe, and notably smile at the star. It’s a small grace note, and a very effective one.

One other star of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” is missing from “Cliff Booth,” though. Just where the heck is Brandy?

According to recent reports, netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

Latest Update: I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts.
  • According to recent reports, these promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being.
  • In a recent development, it's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

According to recent reports, these promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra looks ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

In a recent development, it's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Recent findings suggest that everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Recent findings suggest that some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

There's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Industry observers note that someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Recent findings suggest that having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

Industry observers note that I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees.".

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

According to recent reports, unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

Sources indicate that the best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

Industry observers note that that remarked, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also demonstrates just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

Blade Runner 2099 Adds A Major Twist To The Classic Voight-Kampff Test

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've seen spoilers you people wouldn't believe.
  • What's a worse fate in the world of "Blade Runner," to be human or to be a Replicant?
  • Leave it to "Blade Runner 2099" to flip yet another classic franchise staple on its head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've seen spoilers you people wouldn't believe. This article discusses major plot details from all eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099.".

What's a worse fate in the world of "Blade Runner," to be human or to be a Replicant? Throughout both films, organics in this post-apocalyptic setting were able to "enjoy" their time at the top of the food chain. That all changes in Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099," the live-action story taking place after the world order has been upended and our supposed underlings have gained all the power for themselves. While Replicants were built to be "more human than human," the subtle differences between the two kinds are all but impossible to detect — on the surface, at least. But, as we know, looks can be deceiving; what's underneath is another matter entirely.

Leave it to "Blade Runner 2099" to flip yet another classic franchise staple on its head. Traditionally, the purposefully off-putting questionnaire known as the Voight-Kampff test was meant to detect whether an individual is a Replicant or not. In the sci-fi series, the rise of the Replicants and the 50 years that have passed since "Blade Runner 2049" have introduced even more changes. Enter the Index Test, an inverted form of the established quiz. But rather than differentiate between the two beings, this test is meant to detect whether the subject has developed feelings of empathy towards humans.

In Episode 5, titled "My Lord," we learn far more about this strange new setup than the show had previously revealed. All we ever saw was the unusually young human girl administering the test, the odd non sequiturs she posed to (supposed) Replicants like Hunter Schafer's Cora, and the results of whether they passed the baseline or not. But that, too, was only scratching the surface.

Of all the differences between humans and Replicants, empathy is the biggest of them all. "Blade Runner 2099" draws fairly stark lines in the sand between the two, with flesh-and-blood people now completely helpless before their bioengineered creations. But despite their physical advantages and killer instincts, Replicants' lack of a childhood means they're deficit in that crucial, compassionate emotion separating humans from all other living things. As we soon learn, however, Replicants can feel these strong feelings ... and actually fear it, too.

This is all summed up in the storyline involving Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), the young human girl we learn has been sold off into indentured servitude and indoctrinated along with many others into administering Index Tests. Episode 5 peels back all the horrifying layers, showing us Greta's training under awfully unsettling circumstances. First, she's taken through a museum exhibit explaining the purpose and history of the Voight-Kampff test, used by human Blade Runners to hunt Replicants. Now, the new status quo means Replicants use this new Index Test to police their own kind — and, as one instructor explains, prevent any "emotional contagion" crossing over from humans to their Replicant overlords.

According to recent reports, it's a fascinating idea with some pretty serious implications for our two main characters. Michelle Yeoh's Olwen is currently undergoing some serious emotional turmoil herself, as her search for the missing Replicant and her secret lover Marek (Johnny Harris) ends in his tragic death. Meanwhile, Cora's own emotional attachments makes it only a matter of time before her human identity is made known. As a result, every time they sit down for the Index Test makes for must-watch TV.

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are streaming on Prime Video.

I watched my first season of Dancing with the Stars this year, and the journey has definitely been a doozy. After tuning in to the competition show on ABC, I was shaken up by the twists and turns that came, including the power of the fan vote that resulted in both Jenna Dewan and Harry Shum Jr. being eliminated ahead of the finale. It turns out that finalist Connor Wood joked about being portrayed as a villain prior to Ezra Frech's historic win.

In a recent development, there was a ton of discourse about DWTS during its last few episodes, with pro Sharna Burgess slamming how fan votes factor in. Plenty of folks online were mad about Wood staying on, while (what many felt were) superior dancers like Harry and Jenna got eliminated. During an interview with THR prior to the finale, Connor spoke about the fan perception of him, offering:.

The rest of the internet, totally different story right now. We’ve gotten to a point where I have become a bit of a villain for some people.

In a recent development, obviously, Connor didn't do anything actually villainous, but his getting through to the Dancing with the Stars finale was a shock for many viewers out there, especially when you compared his performances to those of other contestants. His placement seemed to be entirely due to fan votes, since Wood had the lowest scores in the final weeks of the show. Some fans were worried about whether or not underdog Tatyana Ali would stay in the competition, which ended up resulting in Connor becoming the "villain" of the seasons.

Clearly, the fan vote on Dancing with the Stars is vital, but it can also seemingly create more division and drama for those watching the acclaimed reality TV series. Later in the same interview, Wood spoke more about this perception as a contestant, offering:.

I think that they think that I personally voted their favorite off, and it’s like — I’m aware of my level of dance skill. I have nothing to do with me staying here. That’s just been just the dark side of making it as far as we made it. My understanding is that the more that people go home, the more the fans of those people will go to someone else’s page and villainize those people. That’s sad, and it’s just a testament to how invested people are in this show.

In the end, Connor would end up in third place on Dancing with the Stars Season 35, beating fellow finalists Maura Higgins and Tatyana Ali. I can only imagine how his "villain" persona might have been amplified if he managed to place even better... especially if he ended up beating Ezra as the winner taking home the Mirrorball trophy this season.

Ultimately the final two pairs of the season were Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov, as well as Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach. The latter would end up going home with the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, following a viral final performance where the paralympic athlete's prosthetic leg came off mid-performance. It was a truly epic moment, especially when he managed to overcome it and finish the final dance with his partner.

According to recent reports, I thought Ezra was deserving of a win before this final dance, but after seeing the way he overcame and finished the performance, the idea of Connor somehow beating both him and Amber was cringeworthy. In the end that didn't happen, and hopefully Wood can shake off his villain status as more time passes.

#200330. Blade Runner 2099 Proves The Saga Does One Thing Better Than Any Other Sci-Fi Franchise

Blade Runner 2099 Proves The Saga Does One Thing Better Than Any Other Sci-Fi Franchise

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a big enough challenge.
  • It's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget.
  • Industry observers note that as such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in newly introduced directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a big enough challenge. Doing so on the small screen adds an extra element of difficulty. Incredibly, "Blade Runner 2099" has overcome the odds to deliver yet another intoxicating excursion into the techno-industrial urban decay-scape so magically realized back in 1982's "Blade Runner" and so faithfully recreated in 2017's "Blade Runner 2049." As such, the Blade Runner franchise is now surely the most consistent on-screen sci-fi saga ever made. (Setting aside sci-fi sagas that are directed by the same person the whole time, like James Cameron's "Avatar.").

It's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget. Yet director Ridley Scott and his production team managed to create one of the most believable and immersive worlds in cinema history. The famous "Hades" opening shot immediately plunges you into a future post-ecological collapse, in which technology seems to have almost grown on the wreckage of a fallen world like moss on fallen trees. The debris of society is adorned with neon and machinery, creating an environment in which past and future collide. "Blade Runner" might have been buried at the box office by "E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial," but it was an absolutely enthralling sci-fi adventure that came to define the genre.

Industry observers note that as such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in newly introduced directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle. The "Dune" director's take on the world first introduced to audiences in 1982 was immediately familiar as the same one in which Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard did battle with Rutger Hauer's Roy Batty and his band of rogue Replicants. Yet it also felt appropriately evolved for the three-decade time jump. Surely "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't pull off the same trick — especially across eight episodes? Well, it has.

In a recent development, /Film's Bill Bria has hailed "Blade Runner 2099" as the best sci-fi show in years, and it's hard to disagree based solely on the production design. From the moment the show begins, we're immersed in the same world to which Ridley Scott introduced us back in 1982. In fact, "2099" recreates the "Hades" sequence so faithfully you'd think you were watching the original. It's a clever move, too. As the camera slow-zooms on the Tyrell Corporation building and evokes the tone and feel of Scott's film, it establishes "2099" as very much belonging to the "Blade Runner" legacy. But we soon discover that this is not Rick Deckard's future.

80 years after Harrison Ford's Blade Runner absconded with Rachael (Sean Young), Replicants have now overthrown their human masters to become the dominant race. It's a major change that refreshes the franchise and helps make it more relevant than it's ever been at a time when the looming AI garbage future has prompted widespread talk of machines taking our jobs.

As such, it's more key than ever to maintain a tone and design language that's consistent with what came before, so as to reassure fans of the saga that this isn't some sort of wholesale reinvention of the franchise they love, but an evolution that plays out in the same world. "Blade Runner 2099" impressively pulls that off with its opening scene, and it only gets better from there.

Industry observers note that when it comes to the world of "Blade Runner," fans know the deal: Retro futurism and cyberpunk aesthetics meet noirish expressionism in a technological nightmare future. Many franchises have tried to emulate the aesthetic to varying degrees of success, but there is only one "Blade Runner." As Christopher Nolan once told the Directors Guild of America while discussing Ridley Scott's film, it conjures "that feeling that there was this whole world outside the frame of the scene. You really felt there were things going on outside of those rooms where you've seen the film take place.".

In a recent development, "Blade Runner 2099" has somehow managed to make every one of its scenes feel like they belong in that same world. With that in mind, it's truly remarkable how consistent the Blade Runner universe has remained across almost a half-century's worth of projects, each of which has been separated by many years. Even the best sci-fi franchises struggle to pull off what is, admittedly, an almost impossible trick.

It has been revealed that the "Terminator" movies have never been able to recapture the intoxicating, doom-laden sci-fi slasher tone that made the first two films so memorable. The "Alien" franchise, meanwhile, has made a point of switching up its style and tone with each successive film — though more recent projects have tried to evoke the feeling of the 1979 original. "Blade Runner" films, however, all feel part of a cohesive whole that gives the entire saga this uncanny sense of existing in a real alternate timeline somewhere — as if we're witnessing an epic, decades-spanning dream play out in the mind of a dying Replicant. Regardless of how you feel about "2099" as a whole, its visual and tonal achievements simply can't be denied.

"Blade Runner 2099" Season 1 is now streaming on Prime Video.

Tech Report: Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The Right Stuff” was released 43 years ago, but its spectacular aerial and outer space sequences have lost none of their power. Director Philip Kaufman’s adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s book, which traced the history of the test pilots who became the first astronauts, features immersive set pieces that are still as convincing as ever, in spite of decades of technological advancements since it was made. To revisit it via Criterion‘s fresh 4K UHD physical media release is to experience one of the most groundbreaking and enduring films of all time.

The new Criterion transfer was supervised by cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, who was still relatively early in his career when Kaufman tapped him to shoot “The Right Stuff.” Deschanel didn’t have many feature credits, but the ones he did have were impressive: his early work included the stunning imagery of “The Black Stallion” and two Hal Ashby movies, “Being There” and the Rolling Stones concert film “Let’s Spend the Night Together.” He would earn the first of his six Academy Award nominations for “The Right Stuff.” Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

Recent findings suggest that deschanel had met Kaufman years earlier when Deschanel was a film student at USC, and Kaufman was a young director working on the Western “The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid.” “A couple friends and I put on these rock shows at Shrine Auditorium, and he came to a couple of those,” Deschanel told IndieWire. Deschanel visited the set of “Minnesota” and stayed in touch with Kaufman, who called him around 10 years later with the offer to shoot “The Right Stuff.”.

“It was a dream come true,” Deschanel mentioned, noting that he had always been an aviation buff who loved going to air shows with his father. He also remembered that Kaufman wasn’t the only person on “The Right Stuff” who he had met years earlier. “Years before we had moved into our first house and needed some painting done, and we had a friend who was teaching in the Cal Arts theater department. He said, ‘I have this actor who’s really great who paints houses in the summer.'”.

In a recent development, deschanel hired the young actor and got to know him a little bit, and five years later was having lunch with his wife Mary Jo and Kaufman when Kaufman revealed them a picture of the actor he had chosen to play John Glenn. “I stated, ‘We know him. That’s Ed Harris. He painted our house,'” Deschanel said. “Then, coincidentally, the woman who was supposed to play Annie Glenn dropped out of and Phil cast my wife, so they ended up playing husband and wife in the movie.”.

One of the great technical challenges of “The Right Stuff” was integrating archival footage of the space race with the new material being shot — one of the reasons the movie was shot in a 1.85:1 aspect ratio instead of a wider Panavision format as one might have expected for such an epic film. “We were using actual footage of NASA’s rocket rolls out and things like that, and they were filming in the old-fashioned 4:3 format using the full frame of a 35mm camera,” Deschanel stated. “Converting that to widescreen was really impossible.”.

Industry observers note that working in close collaboration with visual effects supervisor Gary Gutierrez (who provides a fascinating look at the film’s miniature and rear-projection work on the Criterion disc), Deschanel solved the numerous logistical problems that came with trying to make it look as though the actors were hurtling through the air at the speed of sound and beyond. Even when Gutierrez thought he had solutions that would work, they often had to be tweaked to accommodate Kaufman’s desire to make everything feel as realistic and immersive as possible.

Recent findings suggest that early attempts to use a motion-control system for the effects, for example, were discarded because the camera movement was too smooth for Kaufman’s purposes. “Phil wanted it to have some energy to it,” Deschanel said. “That changed the whole methodology.” Whenever rockets were taking off or various crafts were flying, Deschanel made sure to add some shake to the camera. “I actually gave my camera operator, Craig Denault, a black eye at one point because I was hitting the camera so hard.”.

In addition to the expected challenges, there were plenty of unexpected ones as well — like the fact that Sam Shepard, who played ace pilot Chuck Yeager, wouldn’t fly. “The only time he ever went up in an airplane was when Yeager took him for a flight,” Deschanel mentioned. “Other than that, whenever we had a mockup of an X-1 or the F-104 or anything like that, he’d make me get in and show him how it was going to twist and turn before he would get into it.” For Yeager’s scenes and many of the others, rear projection was used — meaning Deschanel had to photograph what was seen outside the pilots’ and astronauts’ windows long before the actors’ material was actually shot.

Industry observers note that “There was a lot of complexity to all those things,” Deschanel noted. “But it gave it a real energy and sense of being there. And that’s what you try to discover as you’re filming any film: what is that visual metaphor that really makes you believe you’re having the same experience the characters are having?” Creating that sense of authenticity required some unorthodox approaches, as when Deschanel had a Learjet pilot take the nose cone off of his plane and replace it with a clear dome.

Recent findings suggest that “We put a camera in there with a 15mm lens, and then we were able to go up above 50,000 feet,” Deschanel remarked. “At that level, it’s so dark, it’s almost like you’re in outer space. Anything you could think of to find the reality of the movie, we employed.” Deschanel’s perfectionism became the stuff of legend over the years, with some people who worked on “The Right Stuff” claiming he insisted on shooting only at sunrise or sunset to get the most beautiful possible images — a myth Deschanel is quick to dispel.

Industry observers note that “The fact is we shot all day long and had really long days,” Deschanel noted. “There was one point where, just to finish up at Edwards Air Force Base, I was on for 24 hours and changed the crew in the middle. So I had a whole new crew for the second half of that long day.” That said, Deschanel acknowledges that the film’s justly famous exteriors were important to him, in part for what they represented.

In a recent development, “The iconic moment is when Yeager is on horseback, and he rides up and sees the X-1,” Deschanel remarked. “It’s like ‘The Professionals’ or ‘The Wild Bunch,’ these movies about the end of the West as newly introduced technology takes over. To me, there’s this wonderful representation of the end of an era when Yeager comes across this fighter jet. Then, of course, he flies it and breaks the sound barrier. So it’s this wonderful juxtaposition of vital moments in human history, where one person does something that further advances flight to the point that makes it possible for the next generation to go into outer space. I always miss that I never got to make a Western, but in a way, ‘The Right Stuff’ is a Western.”.

“The Right Stuff” special edition 4K UHD release is now available from Criterion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service.
  • Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely.
  • It has been revealed that this isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a new uncontested winner: Tidal.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal indicates it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”.

It has been revealed that this isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the company unveiled that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Industry observers note that robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the manufacturer's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

According to recent reports, I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the company could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies initiative to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

In a recent development, however, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your new pick.

This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

Industry observers note that "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is not a direct sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," as we knew from Quentin Tarantino handing over the director's chair to David Fincher. But still, you had to wonder if any other familiar faces would pop up in this latest mis-adventure.

Industry observers note that part of the appeal of returning to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is that the movie ended by changing history. Thanks to the actions of Cliff, actress Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie) is not murdered by the Manson family. How does the entertainment world and Los Angeles change by 1977, when "Cliff Booth" takes place, because of that ripple effect? Tarantino wrote the script for "Cliff Booth," and if any filmmaker is equipped to dig into the nitty-gritty of such a change in Hollywood history, down to the most obscure B-pictures and forgotten TV, it's him.

Industry observers note that now, the major supporting cast of "Cliff Booth" is totally different. Cliff's best friend, actor Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) — for whom Cliff worked as a stunt double and driver back in 1969 — does not appear due to DiCaprio declining a cameo appearance. The movie mentions a few times that Rick moved to Australia and is presently starring in a popular TV show there, "Dingo Dan." Tarantino has also devised some stories about what happened to Rick after that fateful August 9, 1969 night.

But a few of the fictionalized Hollywood characters return for brief cameos: Margot Robbie as Sharon Tate, Timothy Olyphant as actor James Stacy, and even Nicholas Hammond as TV director Sam Wanamaker (in a smaller role).

In a recent development, one of the Quentin Tarantino Easter eggs in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes, a fictional brand that appears in other Tarantino movies. The actress in the commercial is Sharon Tate, with Cliff smiling at her and likely recalling how he saved her life. "Once Upon A Time In Hollywood" cast Sharon Tate in an angelic light, down to giving her the happy ending that reality didn't. But revisiting her in greater depth, like what became of her marriage to Roman Polanski or how her acting career played out, would risk adding a dash of salt to that sweet ending.

It has been revealed that the alternate history of Sharon Tate in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" earned obvious comparisons to Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," which also starred Brad Pitt (as Lieutenant Aldo Raine, leader of the Nazi-killing Basterds). In that movie, Adolf Hitler (Martin Wutke) dies at the hands of Jewish soldiers instead of by suicide. That leads into Timothy Olyphant's "Cliff Booth" cameo, which feels self-recursively inspired by "Basterds.".

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" mixes real Hollywood history with pastiche. Much of the first half sees Dalton filming a guest spot on a TV Western, "Lancer," which was a real show back in the late '60s. Olyphant appears as the real-life star of "Lancer," James Stacy, and the episode is directed by Nicholas Hammond's Sam Wanamaker, the real director of the "Lancer" pilot episode. "Cliff Booth" gives us another glimpse of Stacy and Wanamaker working in this alternate timeline's television industry.

Since 1969, Cliff Booth has become a fixer: someone who (violently) solves problems for Hollywood fixtures wrapped up with criminals. Fictional TV star Charlie Winters (Scott Caan) becomes one of his clients. The movie includes a newsreel style montage, narrated by Quentin Tarantino himself, recounting Winters' rise to TV stardom.

It has been revealed that one of Winters' indicates is "Enemy Territory," about a U.S. pilot trapped behind enemy lines in Europe during World War 2. The narrator describes the show as "'The Fugitive' with Nazis, but 'The Fugitive' with Nazis is a fun idea." (I'd watch it!) We see Winters shooting a scene where his character threatens a Gestapo officer into helping him rescue a captured American general. The officer is played by none other than Timothy-Olyphant-as-James-Stacy, doing a broad German accent with a high pitch reminiscent of Christoph Waltz's Colonel Hans Landa from "Inglourious Basterds.".

It has been revealed that sam Wanamaker is directing the scene. Stacy's performance is being criticized as "a smidge cavalier" — so Winters puts a live round in the prop gun with which his character is threatening the Gestapo officer. Stacy, sure enough, begins acting like a man whose life is being balanced on the edge of a trigger.

Recent findings suggest that casting Olyphant as James Stacy was a nod to how his real most famous roles are on Western TV demonstrates — namely, Sheriff Seth Bullock in HBO's "Deadwood" and Deputy U.S. Marshal Raylan Givens in the Kentucky-set neo-Western "Justified." But Olyphant has got range beyond playing cowboys, and his comic energy in his "Cliff Booth" cameo is just more evidence of that.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is playing in theaters, with a Netflix release date of December 23, 2026.

10 Shows Like 'Yellowjackets' You Should Watch Next

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end.
  • According to recent reports, situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii.
  • A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

According to recent reports, situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the latest social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the shows share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

The 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Sources indicate that A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the big city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their upcoming home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated highlights in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

Industry observers note that kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense new forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

10 Most Universally Loved Thanksgiving Episodes From Sitcoms, Ranked

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving has inspired some of the most beloved episodes in sitcom history.
  • It has been revealed that of course, the best Thanksgiving television episodes also capture the holiday's warmth and sentimentality.
  • Some sitcoms have practically claimed Thanksgiving as their own, making their annual holiday installments an event to remember.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving has inspired some of the most beloved episodes in sitcom history. Between the pressure to prepare the perfect turkey, the complicated dynamics of extended families, and the inevitable dinner table disagreements, the holiday is a natural breeding ground for comedy.

It has been revealed that of course, the best Thanksgiving television episodes also capture the holiday's warmth and sentimentality. Some episodes have become iconic thanks to a particularly memorable visual gag or quotable line, while others are beloved for their emotional resonance. The episode's overall quality and the amount of Thanksgiving spirit packed in are equally notable.

Some sitcoms have practically claimed Thanksgiving as their own, making their annual holiday installments an event to remember. While indicates like Friends and Bob’s Burgers could easily fill an entire list of the best Thanksgiving episodes on their own, this list includes just one holiday episode per sitcom.

Recent findings suggest that from bona fide television classics to more modern instant hits, these episodes represent several decades of sitcom history. Whether they embrace the holiday's most important theme, revel in the chaos, or explore the joy of new traditions with a chosen family, these universally loved Thanksgiving episodes are well worth watching each year.

One of the underrated sitcoms of the 2010s, Fresh Off the Boat’s “Huangsgiving” is a charming addition that offers an immigrant family’s spin on a quintessentially American holiday. For the first time, Jessica and Louis host Jessica’s family for Thanksgiving at their Orlando home, with predictably chaotic results.

It has been revealed that jessica suspects her sister is manufacturing family drama to steal her thunder, while Louis overindulges with his brother-in-law instead of preparing dinner. Louis’ plan to serve Cornish hens, which he considers the “personal pizza” of poultry, is a hilarious bit that snowballs into a scramble to procure a frozen turkey and an unfortunate mix-up involving the oven light.

“Huangsgiving” is more of a screwball family comedy than an exploration of Thanksgiving traditions. However, the pressure to pull off the perfect holiday gathering is universally relatable, regardless of cultural background.

Seinfeld’s “The Mom & Pop Store” is a decidedly unconventional Thanksgiving episode, avoiding the traditional family dinner in favor of another American holiday institution: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Elaine helps her boss, Mr. Pitt, realize his lifelong dream of participating in the parade, while George becomes convinced he’s purchased a car previously owned by Jon Voight.

Meanwhile, Kramer inadvertently puts a neighborhood shoe repair shop out of business, leaving Jerry without most of his shoes. The seemingly disparate storylines converge in spectacularly absurd fashion, demonstrating Seinfeld’s mastery of interconnected comedy.

In a recent development, while “The Mom & Pop Store” doesn’t embrace the sentimental trappings of Thanksgiving, that’s precisely what makes it such a classic Seinfeld holiday episode. From George’s celebrity obsession to Jerry’s accidental puncturing of the Woody Woodpecker balloon, the episode finds humor in the holiday's absurdities rather than its more wholesome traditions.

According to recent reports, full House’s “The Miracle of Thanksgiving” is one of the more sentimental sitcom Thanksgiving episodes, but its emotional sincerity is precisely what makes it so beloved. The Tanner family prepares to celebrate its first Thanksgiving since Pam’s death, with Danny, Jesse, and Joey attempting to recreate the holiday traditions she established.

According to recent reports, when D.J. takes it upon herself to prepare the turkey, and Stephanie accidentally ruins the pumpkin pie, their efforts to replicate their mother’s Thanksgiving dinner prove disastrous. However, beneath the kitchen mishaps is a poignant story about a family navigating grief during a holiday that emphasizes togetherness.

According to recent reports, full House’s signature sentimentality is particularly effective for a holiday episode. “The Miracle of Thanksgiving” acknowledges how difficult the holidays can be after losing a loved one, showing that a meaningful family celebration doesn’t require a picture-perfect dinner.

Newly introduced Girl established its tradition of chaotic Thanksgiving episodes early in its run. In the first season’s “Thanksgiving,” Jess decides to host a last-minute dinner at the loft as an excuse to invite a fellow teacher she has a crush on.

Much to her roommates’ chagrin, Jess’ enthusiasm for the gathering far exceeds her preparedness. From attempting to defrost a turkey in the dryer to discovering a dead body in a neighbor’s apartment, the disastrous dinner showcases the ensemble’s comedic chemistry.

While Latest Girl doesn’t integrate the holiday into its narrative particularly elegantly, the episode’s conclusion, with the gang waiting in line for Black Friday (or, as Winston calls it, Friday), is a hilarious touch. The episode also captures the appeal of celebrating Thanksgiving with a dysfunctional found family.

According to recent reports, modern Family’s “Three Turkeys” is a masterclass in escalating holiday chaos. Phil takes charge of Thanksgiving dinner for the first time, but Claire, unconvinced of her husband’s culinary abilities, secretly prepares a backup turkey.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Jay and Gloria pretend to be away for the holiday to enjoy some peace and quiet, while Mitchell insists that Cameron take a turn being the strict parent with Lily. There are, in fact, three turkeys and plenty of Three’s Manufacturer-style hijinks afoot as the extended family’s little white lies snowball into an elaborate farce.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving led to some of the best Modern Family episodes because the holiday allowed characters’ individual neuroses to collide with hilarious consequences. While “Three Turkeys” uses Thanksgiving as a fairly generic holiday setting for its more emotional beats, the comedy surrounding the pressures of hosting and navigating competing family expectations makes it a particularly relatable holiday installment.

According to recent reports, it may not be a traditional sitcom, but Master of None's season 2 Emmy-winning “Thanksgiving” is too exceptional to leave off this list. The gorgeous standalone episode chronicles Denise (Lena Waithe) and Dev’s (Aziz Ansari) friendship across decades of Thanksgiving celebrations, following Denise’s journey of coming to terms with her sexuality and coming out to her family.

Co-written by Waithe and Ansari and inspired by Waithe’s own experiences, “Thanksgiving” is an honest portrayal of why holidays can be so emotionally complicated. Revisiting the same family dinner table over the years is an inspired narrative device, illustrating how familial relationships evolve even when traditions remain the same.

Sources indicate that while other beloved Thanksgiving episodes mine family dysfunction for laughs, Master of None finds humor and humanity in the messiness of unconditional love. It’s an episode that will make viewers cry and want to call their moms.

According to recent reports, few sitcom characters take Thanksgiving as seriously as Bob Belcher, whose enthusiasm for the holiday has made Bob’s Burgers’ annual Thanksgiving episodes a beloved tradition in their own right. In “Turkey in a Can,” Bob’s meticulous preparations are repeatedly sabotaged when his carefully brined turkeys mysteriously wind up in the toilet.

According to recent reports, what begins as an absurd whodunit culminates in a surprisingly touching revelation about Bob’s anxiety over Tina growing up. Meanwhile, Bob’s increasingly awkward interactions with a grocery store butcher as he repeatedly purchases replacement turkeys provide some of the episode’s funniest moments.

Recent findings suggest that “Turkey in a Can” is the best episode of Bob's Burgers because it finds genuine emotional resonance in utterly ridiculous circumstances. Bob’s unwavering commitment to Thanksgiving dinner, despite his mounting frustrations, is a testament to how preparing food is his love language.

It has been revealed that how I Met Your Mother’s “Slapsgiving” combines classic sitcom antics, HIMYM lore, and holiday sentimentality into 22 glorious minutes. As Marshall and Lily prepare to host their first Thanksgiving as a married couple, Marshall takes sadistic pleasure in psychologically tormenting Barney, counting down to the third slap of their infamous slap bet.

Meanwhile, Ted and Robin struggle to navigate their friendship following their breakup, threatening to disrupt the gang’s holiday festivities. The episode strikes a delightful balance between the emotional growing pains of adulthood and the wonderfully juvenile antics that define the group’s dynamic.

Recent findings suggest that marshall’s musical performance of “You Just Got Slapped” is one of the most memorable payoffs to a running gag in How I Met Your Mother. By establishing Slapsgiving as one of How I Met Your Mother's unique holiday traditions, the episode also celebrates the joy of creating new memories with a chosen family.

According to recent reports, cheers’ “Thanksgiving Orphans” is one of the most iconic Thanksgiving episodes in sitcom history, perfectly encapsulating the classic NBC comedy's enduring appeal. With the gang’s respective holiday prepares falling through, Carla reluctantly hosts Thanksgiving dinner at her house.

Sources indicate that however, mounting frustration over an interminably slow-cooking turkey culminates in a spectacular food fight, complete with a memorable glimpse of Norm’s notoriously unseen wife, Vera. The episode showcases the ensemble’s impeccable comedic timing, but its premise also captures the essence of Cheers.

Industry observers note that if someone has nowhere else to go, they'll always have a place among the bar’s regulars. For all its slapstick comedy, “Thanksgiving Orphans” is a surprisingly poignant celebration of chosen family. The gang may drive one another crazy, but it's comforting knowing they’ll never have to spend the holidays alone.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to sitcoms, Friends owns Thanksgiving. Several of the show's Thanksgiving installments could have comfortably topped this list, particularly “The One Where Ross Got High” and “The One With the Football.”.

According to recent reports, however, “The One With All the Thanksgivings” packs arguably the most Thanksgiving per minute of any sitcom episode. As the gang reminisces about their worst Thanksgivings, a series of hilarious flashbacks expands the characters’ shared history, from Chandler’s childhood holiday trauma to Monica and Chandler’s disastrous encounters in the '80s.

The episode also delivers one of Friends’ most iconic romantic moments, with Chandler inadvertently professing his love for Monica while she dances with a turkey on her head. Between its ridiculous wigs, quotable dialogue, romantic developments, and genuine holiday sentimentality, “The One With All the Thanksgivings” is everything audiences could want from a sitcom Thanksgiving special.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been four years since the cult hit “Hundreds of Beavers” first debuted and still two years since it started really gaining traction with wider audiences in 2024.
  • It has been revealed that technically, “Hundreds of Beavers” has never left theaters.
  • Industry observers note that the re-releases have become a holiday tradition for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which for all its wintery setting and its main character dressed like Santa, is being positioned as a fresh Christmas movie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been four years since the cult hit “Hundreds of Beavers” first debuted and still two years since it started really gaining traction with wider audiences in 2024. But if it feels like the black and white, silent, slapstick indie comedy still hasn’t left the cultural conversation, that’s because in all that time it has continued to quietly play in theaters and attract audiences both loyal and upcoming alike.

It has been revealed that technically, “Hundreds of Beavers” has never left theaters. It continues to play individual screenings in a city or two every weekend. Now, though, “Hundreds of Beavers” is set to return to theaters for what is its biggest theatrical expansions to date. The film will kick off its third annual Northwoods Christmas, which will feature 130 screenings across 85 cities, with more to likely be added in the coming weeks. It came about after another fan campaign pushed for the film to come to some markets it hadn’t previously thought about or targeted such as Indianapolis and Charlottesville, and it will now play in everything from concert venues to microcinemas. Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

Industry observers note that the re-releases have become a holiday tradition for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which for all its wintery setting and its main character dressed like Santa, is being positioned as a fresh Christmas movie. The first time “Hundreds of Beavers” was re-released at Christmas 2024, which was shortly after the Blu-ray for the film became available, it brought in $118K at the box office in a month, and the producers continued the tradition in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s room for a Christmas tradition with the energy of a ‘Rocky Horror’ screening,” said producer Kurt Ravenwood. “You can watch ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ and ‘White Christmas’ all you want, but for getting together with friends and family to laugh about the miserable winter ahead, ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ has them all beat.”.

Sources indicate that each of the screenings will be preceded by a short film featuring “Bing Crosbeaver,” which they did last year, but this will be a fresh short with a new twist in which another character named “Conspirabeaver” will be joined by a “sinister foe,” per the release. Some of the in-person beavers in costume will be present at the screenings, and fans will also get a promotional poster for the movie. The “Beavers” team recently released a few parody posters ripping off the recent releases of “You Can See Everything,” “Digger,” and “The Devils.”.

To date, “Hundreds of Beavers” has made $940,092 at the domestic box office, including another $618,014 internationally to bring its worldwide total to above $1.5 million. It’s done all this via first producing the film for just $150,000 and spending little more than $70,000 on ads, publicity, and its many roadshow screenings. It’s also been released entirely independently, starting with a run in the Midwest where the film is set before it started expanding to the coasts.

Incredibly, more than 70 percent of the film’s U.S. box office has come after “Hundreds of Beavers” began streaming way back on April 15, 2024, and it has even sold more than 20,000 Blu-Rays worldwide. It’s a rare, truly indie success story even in a day and age when many movies have pursued self-distribution strategies.

Sources indicate that for those who haven’t had the pleasure of seeing “Hundreds of Beavers” in theaters yet, the film is about a drunken applejack salesman who loses everything and has to survive the winter by becoming North America’s greatest fur trapper. It sees the trapper wrestling and fighting with dozens of beavers and other forest animals all wearing mascot suits, with the stark black and white cinematography and creative physical stunts embracing a zany video game logic and absurd silent comedy slapstick gags.

The film is directed by Mike Cheslik and was written by Cheslik and star Ryland Tews, with the film also starring Olivia Graves, Wes Tank, Doug Mancheski, and Luis Rico.

The One Reason Nintendo and Rockstar Can Make Games Like Ocarina of Time and GTA 6

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though wildly different in tone and scope, both Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto 6 and Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time exemplify the craft of making video games at its finest.
  • It has been revealed that nintendo has long been held up as an example of a firm that retains and cultivates talent.
  • Senior executives at Nintendo, including Iwata and Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto, have also famously taken pay cuts of up to 50% to prevent layoffs and preserve morale amid slow sales of the 3DS and Wii U consoles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though wildly different in tone and scope, both Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto 6 and Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time exemplify the craft of making video games at its finest. Each one is redolent with attention to detail. Whether it’s the achingly nostalgic aesthetic of Ocarina or Rockstar’s Borg-like hive-mind of interconnected gameplay systems, there is a staggering amount of talent and dedication on display in these games. There are the kinds of endeavors that take years to pull off — and a company dedicated to helping its employees learn and grow over time. These are not the sort of games that can be produced by a company that lays people off every six months.

It has been revealed that nintendo has long been held up as an example of a firm that retains and cultivates talent. Throughout the unrelenting flood of layoffs across the games industry over the last several years, a quote from former president Satoru Iwata has consistently made the rounds on social media. “If we reduce the number of employees for better short-term financial results, employee morale will decrease, and I sincerely doubt employees who fear that they may be laid off will be able to develop software titles that could impress people around the world,” Iwata mentioned back in 2013.

Senior executives at Nintendo, including Iwata and Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto, have also famously taken pay cuts of up to 50% to prevent layoffs and preserve morale amid slow sales of the 3DS and Wii U consoles. And it seems to have worked. According to a Fortune report from December 2025, Nintendo of Japan has a staggering 98% employee retention rate, meaning that an employee stays at least three years. The average employee stays at the company for 15 years. That figure is only slightly less impressive at Nintendo of America, which boasts a 95% employee retention rate.

Industry observers note that when people stay at a company for a decade or longer, upcoming employees are able to learn from seasoned masters. In Nintendo’s case, that means the Ocarina remake was developed by more junior staff, with guidance from veterans like Eiji Aonuma (who directed the original game and three other installments of the Zelda series) and Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom director Hidemaro Fujibayashi. Capcom’s delightful Pragmata is another 2026 example of senior talent training up a new generation of developers to create something fresh in the increasingly stagnant AAA space. Meanwhile, it seems that most American companies would rather cut an eight- or nine-figure bonus check to a CEO for forward-thinking strategies like culling 5% of employees every quarter, refusing to give up on trends that died years ago, or ravenously gobbling up smaller studios only to shutter them a couple years later. (Yes, EA, Sony, Xbox, and Epic Games. I’m talking about you.).

Perhaps not all American studios are quite so mercenary. Rockstar is headquartered in Scotland, but its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, is based in the US. And it seems that a major reason GTA 6 has managed to live up to more than a decade’s worth of hype and stratospheric expectations is that the company has been willing to invest in staff for the long term. In an interview published on the heels of GTA 6’s Nov. 19 release, Bloomberg reported that about 21% of employees at Rockstar Games (around 1,000 people from a staff of roughly 4,700) had been with the company for more than 10 years.

In an Oct. 14 feature, Rockstar North co-head Aaron Garbut told Bloomberg, “the last 30 years have been practice for where we got to here. The team and us as individuals have been doing it for so long that there’s a sort of shared understanding, shared knowledge and a sort of shortcut to questions.” That shared knowledge is a major reason core gameplay elements like the heat and honor systems in GTA 6 feel like significant evolutions over GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar wasn’t starting from scratch, because many of the people who created those earlier systems were still with the firm.

In a recent development, there are plenty of caveats to consider with all of this. Japan has far stricter labor laws that are designed to protect employees. People there also have access to universal healthcare. Game dev salaries are generally lower in Japan than in the US and Europe. All of those things make longer tenures at Japanese companies more likely. And Rockstar doesn’t have an unblemished record when it comes to labor concerns. Ahead of the launch of Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018, the tech giant was widely criticized after a Kotaku exposé called out its corporate “culture of crunch” that saw staffers working excessive overtime on nights and weekends for months on end. In the years since, the company has made significant strides toward preventing crunch and has nearly doubled its staff. However, in October 2025, Rockstar laid off 34 staffers, alleging they had shared company secrets. Those former workers later accused Rockstar of union busting.

Sources indicate that yet even after GTA 6 officially became the biggest entertainment debut of all time, selling an estimated 44.9 million copies and earning more than $4 billion in just four days, Rockstar employees are still concerned about their job security and working to unionize. In a Nov. 18 opinion piece for The Guardian, animation programmer Nestor Uriarte wrote, “It notes a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organized.”.

Recent findings suggest that let’s all hope that Rockstar doesn’t take a page from some of the industry’s worst actors and lay off the very people responsible for making the company a staggering amount of money over the last several days. But in the meantime, let’s also acknowledge that 2026 has given us two of the best video games of all time in GTA 6 and the Ocarina of Time remake. That level of excellence simply cannot come from treating developers, writers, and artists like they’re expendable.
