The Hunting Wives Season 2 Review: The Steamy Netflix Drama Hits The Mark Again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is.
  • Recent findings suggest that I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment.
  • "The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This review contains discussions of addiction.

I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is. Let's use the original run of "Gossip Girl" as an example. This delightfully dishy show started out as a series about teenagers behaving badly in Newly introduced York City and became a flat-out soap opera — in the best way — where characters marry princes, make deals with God after near-fatal car accidents, and sell each other for hotels. My point is that "Gossip Girl" made a choice, at a certain point, to steer into the proverbial skid and just be as absurd and insane as possible, because the show knew it was high camp, not high art.

Recent findings suggest that I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment. Created by Rebecca Cutter and adapted from May Cobb's book of the same name, "The Hunting Wives" premiered in the summer of 2025 and introduced Netflix audiences to Brittany Snow's Sophie O'Neil, who moves from Cambridge, Massachusetts to the heartland of Texas when her husband Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) gets a lucrative job working for oil tycoon and political hopeful Jed Banks (Dermot Mulroney). When Sophie — who's in recovery as an alcoholic after killing a pedestrian while intoxicated behind the wheel back in Cambridge — encounters Jed's wife Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman), she finds herself drawn into Margo's social circle and drawn to Margo herself, and the two start a torrid affair as teenagers start turning up dead in the seemingly idyllic community of Maple Brook.

"The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever. If you liked how hot and nuts the first season was, you'll be happy to hear Cutter has turned the dial up to 11.

In a recent development, after the Season 1 cliffhanger ending where Sophie accidentally kills Margo's beloved but law-breaking brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), there's a lot to deal with in Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives." Jed is continuing his run for governor, but both he and Graham are furious that their wives cuckolded them; Sophie and Margo are estranged over the fact that Sophie figures out, in the final episode, that Margo is responsible for the death of the teenaged Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe). (Margo isn't one of 2025's best TV villains for nothin'.) Despite this, the two end up in bed together pretty promptly in Season 2, and they're just as hot together as ever; if you loved all of the steamy scenes in "The Hunting Wives" Season 1, rest assured that there's plenty for you to enjoy here.

Industry observers note that across the board, Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" takes everything you loved about Season 1 and delivers it in spades. Guns are blazing, kisses are passionate and steamy, and the interpersonal drama is as wild as ever; Brittany Snow and Malin Åkerman are excellent, once again, as two women locked in a love affair that constantly threatens to derail both of their lives. Even as the stakes get sillier and higher, Snow and Åkerman treat every moment that they're on-screen, separately or together, with the utmost seriousness. Remember what Michael Caine did in "A Muppet Christmas Carol?" That's basically what these two powerhouses actresses are doing in "The Hunting Wives," but with considerably more nudity ... and it rocks. The second outing of "The Hunting Wives" forces Margo and Sophie the most heightened situations imaginable, but thanks to Snow and Åkerman's performances, you believe that they're hopelessly in love.

It has been revealed that my biggest critique of a show as fundamentally unserious as "The Hunting Wives" is that its lack of gravity can brush up against legitimately serious in-universe challenges. By that, I mean Sophie's drinking. Sophie killed someone in a drunk driving accident before this show's story began, and even though the show does make you root for her relationship with Margo, it also seems to want to make a larger point that Sophie is addicted to Margo ... especially because Margo typically pours Sophie a drink when they're together. To call this message muddled would be ... generous.

In a recent development, with all that stated, I would certainly hope that people dealing with addiction aren't looking to a show like "The Hunting Wives" for a realistic portrayal of that glitch. This is also a show where, by the end of Season 2, the body count is in the double digits — and I actually mean that in two senses, because there's a litany of dead bodies and a ton of latest romantic trysts by the time the season finale's credits roll.

Honestly, across the last few episodes of Season 2 — critics received the entire eight-episode season — the number of corpses that pile up gets so out of control that the deaths stopped being shocking and started feeling routine. (Without getting into major spoilers, Brad breaks bad in a big way, and it honestly grows tiresome pretty rapidly.) I still want to be clear, though: "The Hunting Wives" isn't prestige television, and it knows it. It doesn't always need to be impeccable or even make sense. It's fun, and it fulfills that qualification pretty beautifully.

Recent findings suggest that dale Dickey, who's finally getting more recognition after years as a supporting small-screen player thanks to her outstanding supporting turn in the perfect 2026 comedy "Widow's Bay," is a perfect fresh addition to Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" as Zelda Moffitt, the formidable head of a Texan motorcycle gang who has a connection to Margo's past. Soap opera star Kim Matula is excellent as Nadia Kelly, a reality TV producer with an ulterior motive, and John Stamos and Cam Gigandet have small but impactful roles as talent scout Chase Brylan and Zelda's son "Gentle John" Moffitt, respectively.

As much as he made my skin crawl, though, I have to give full credit to "The Wilds" alum Alex Fitzalan, who appears as the conniving campaign manager Lincoln Trout. As Jed's new right-hand man — with an emphasis on the word right — Fitzalan's Lincoln is disgusting, reprehensible, and compulsively watchable. I suspect he'll play a pretty large role in Season 3, and as horrifying as he is writ large, I sort of can't wait to see more.

Speaking of Season 3, the sophomore season of "The Hunting Wives" leaves us with such a good cliffhanger — which did genuinely surprise me after the back half of the season got just a tiny bit bogged down with murder after murder after murder — that I cannot wait until the planned third season is available to watch. "The Hunting Wives" is one of the most patently ridiculous reveals airing right now, and that's not a bad thing at all; in fact, it's exactly what makes it such an incredibly fun ride from start to finish.

"The Hunting Wives" is streaming on Netflix now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, indieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Wednesday, November 25 the final additions to the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

In a recent development, the newly revealed honorees include “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and costume designer Trish Summerville, who will be receiving the Spotlight Award. They join previously announced honorees John Turturro, Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield, Ike Barinholtz, Yura Borisov, James Gray, Adam Driver, Beth de Araújo, Mason Reeves, Gemma Chan, Ruth Madeley, David Greaves, Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo, Jeon Do-yeon, Anthony Ippolito, James Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, Mag Sarnowska, Paul Lambert, and Travis Knight. Related Stories Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Significant Christmas Expansion Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’.

Industry observers note that additionally, IndieWire has announced that the incoming awards ceremony will be hosted by writer and comedian Demi Adejuyigbe, whose latest special “Demi Adejuyigbe Is Going to Do 1 (One) Backflip” is now available to stream on Dropout. Previous IndieWire Honors emcees include Emmy winner Alex Edelman, Emmy nominee Robby Hoffman, multi-hyphenate Dewayne Perkins, and lauded comedians Vinny Thomas and Atsuko Okatsuka.

IndieWire Honors will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well.

Sources indicate that “It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” noted Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”.

Sources indicate that “It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”.

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:.

It has been revealed that the fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

According to recent reports, the pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

It has been revealed that made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

Industry observers note that “Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

According to recent reports, an early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

Sources indicate that the most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Recent findings suggest that re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she stated uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

According to recent reports, all sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

Recent findings suggest that there is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she states. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

In a recent development, as the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

Industry observers note that there is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

According to recent reports, though the latest film from director David Fincher and screenwriter Quentin Tarantino furthers the mis-adventures of Cliff Booth, the role that earned star Brad Pitt an Oscar, the Netflix film has an identity all its own. The work of costume designer Trish Summerville and actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II are two elements that put that into focus, really easing the audience into the jump forward to 1977, where the silks flowed, and fur dripped off new screen icons akin to the latter’s Rodrick “Hot Rod” Harrison. This go-round allows viewers to have an appreciation for more than just Hollywood, but the greater Los Angeles area, and all the distinct styles it brought in that pivotal ‘70s moment.

Sources indicate that ink is based on screenwriter James Graham’s Tony Award-winning play that follows a visionary group of misfits with an idea that would change tabloid journalism and the world as we know it forever. Based on a true story, the movie takes place in 1969, when rising media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, portrayed in the movie by Pearce, acquires the newspaper The Sun. In a team-up with editor Larry Lamb, played by O’Connell, they exploit sensational news to turn their paper into an explosive hit. In addition to O’Connell and Lamb, Ink also stars Claire Foy (The Crown), Jonathan Hyde (The Brutalist), Georgie Henley (The Chronicles of Narnia), and Bertie Carvel (A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms).

If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it.
  • Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not.
  • At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

Sources indicate that it’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that if you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a major payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that the true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

84 Years Later, Casablanca's Best Line Is Still The Most Romantic Quote In Movie History

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you're not familiar with "Casablanca," I have to assume that you're from some sort of alien planet, have been in a coma for decades, or are a newborn baby.
  • That's when Ingrid Bergman's Ilsa Lund walks into Rick's particular gin joint, to sloppily paraphrase one of his best quotes (and we'll circle back to that).
  • "Casablanca" is, admittedly, stacked from top to bottom with memorable quotes (more on that shortly), but "Here's looking at you, kid" feels like it transcends the very film it came from.

According to recent reports, if you're not familiar with "Casablanca," I have to assume that you're from some sort of alien planet, have been in a coma for decades, or are a newborn baby. Directed by Michael Curtiz and written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein, and Howard Koch (whose script adapts the play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison), "Casablanca" centers around the taciturn bar owner Rick Blaine (the incomparable Humphrey Bogart), an American ex-pat living in the titular city in Morocco (which was still a colony of France at the time, as the film is set in December 1941). As Rick accepts refugees and ex-pats of all stripes (and has an anti-Axis and anti-Nazi past of his own), he also quietly ensures paperwork to people looking to escape the Nazi regime.

That's when Ingrid Bergman's Ilsa Lund walks into Rick's particular gin joint, to sloppily paraphrase one of his best quotes (and we'll circle back to that). After Ilsa and Rick had a beautiful love affair in occupied Paris and planned to escape together, Ilsa simply vanished, which gave us the bitter, cynical, and lovelorn Rick we see living in Casablanca. Not only is Ilsa back, but she needs a favor: Her husband Victor Laszlo (Paul Henreid), whom she believed was dead when she romanced Rick in Paris, needs papers to evade the Nazis hunting him so that the couple can run away to Portugal (which is unoccupied). Not only does Rick give Ilsa the papers that she and Victor need, he gives up the woman he loves so that she and Victor can live their lives safely. "Casablanca" is a sweeping story of righteous protest against fascism, lost love, and sacrifice ... and "Here's looking at you, kid" is one of its most memorable lines.

"Casablanca" is, admittedly, stacked from top to bottom with memorable quotes (more on that shortly), but "Here's looking at you, kid" feels like it transcends the very film it came from. There are probably people out there who don't even know that this sweet nothing came from this 1942 classic (and I'd like anyone who doesn't to sit their butt down and watch all of "Casablanca" right now), yet the fact of the matter is that "Here's looking at you, kid" has stood the test of time and remains one of the most immortal lines in movie history.

So, why is that? Rick says this line to Ilsa throughout "Casablanca," and we see him utter it during flashbacks to the couple's happier times in Paris and right before he puts her on the plane with Victor that will take her to Portugal safely. It's simple but unbelievably meaningful. Before understanding why Ilsa suddenly left Paris, Rick was furious that she vanished from his life. When she reveals that she only left because Victor was alive, sick, and needed her help after he escaped from a concentration camp, his heart softens, and he's able to forgive her for the heartbreak she caused. Rick loves Ilsa, and there's no denying that Ilsa loves Rick, but she's in love with Victor — and the film smartly doesn't villainize Victor, making him a genuinely decent guy who simply wants to escape enemy forces and live peacefully with his wife after years of torment. "Here's looking at you, kid" is Rick's expression of love for Ilsa, and him saying it right as he puts her on a plane that will take her away forever is both heartbreaking and romantic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barbara Gordon, the classic Batgirl, gets her coolest art ever, and her iconic costume is nowhere in sight. For close to 60 years, Barbara Gordon has been an integral member of the Bat Family, be it as Batgirl or Oracle. At the moment, Barbara is in the fight of her life in the new Breakout maxiseries, but it also gives her some truly awesome art.

Industry observers note that initially created to tie in with the then in-production Batman television series, Batgirl first appeared in 1967’s Detective Comics #359, debuting in the program around that time as well. The daughter of Commissioner Gordon, Barbara became Batgirl and fought crime alongside Batman and Robin. Then, in 1988’s The Killing Joke, the Joker shot Barbara, paralyzing her from the waist down. Undaunted, Barbara became Oracle, which allowed her to utilize her background in information science, serving as an information broker for the heroes of the DC Universe.

Batgirl was created by television producer William Dozier, writer Gardner Fox, artist Carmine Infantino and editor Julius Schwartz.

In a recent development, barbara resumed her career as Batgirl at the beginning of the Latest 52 era, but has since stepped back from the spotlight. Earlier this year, as part of its Next Level initiative, DC released Barbara Gordon: Breakout. Written by Mariko Tamaki and drawn by Amancay Nahuelpan, Breakout sees Gordon sent to prison. Yet there is far more going on just below the surface, and she is getting to the bottom of it all. It will be a struggle for Barbara, but it is also providing some awesome art in the process.

Sources indicate that DC Comics has released its solicitations for books shipping in February, including Barabra Gordon: Breakout #10, by the book’s regular creative team of Tamaki and Nahuelpan. DC released a plot synopsis for Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10, which reads as follows:.

Barbara Gordon entered Supermax to save inmates from an unknown killer. But after last problem’s shocking revelations, she may have doomed everyone within the prison’s walls. With the clock counting down, can she stop the bloodbath before it begins? Or has her quest to rescue some of the prisoners doomed them all?

The book will ship with variant covers by Taurin Clarke and Francesco Tomaselli.

Of particular interest is the main cover for Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10. Drawn by Jorge Fornes, the cover depicts Gordon, battered and bandaged up, diving from the top of the prison she is being held in, all while a massive explosion happens above her. The implication is Barbara has escaped from prison, and the bad guys have been punished.

According to recent reports, yet perhaps the most noteworthy aspect of the cover for Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10 is what the titular heroine is wearing. Her traditional Batgirl costume is nowhere to be seen. Instead, she wears the standard jumpsuit of an inmate. The sight of the law-abiding Barbara Gordon dressed as a convict might scramble the brains of some, but it actually makes perfect sense.

It has been revealed that the cover to Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10 makes an vital point about the character: that her heroism transcends whatever codename or handle she is using at the time. As a child, she watched her parents drift apart and her brother descend into madness. Witnessing such sights young could have caused Barbara to become a hateful recluse. However, she channeled this anger and outrage in a positive way, becoming Batgirl and one of Bruce’s most trusted allies.

Some fans argue that Barbara did not come into her own until she became Oracle, as it helped her truly escape Batman’s shadow.

Industry observers note that then, when life dealt her a bad hand, she made the best of it by becoming Oracle in 1989’s Suicide Squad #23. Some fans argue that Barbara did not come into her own until she became Oracle, as it helped her truly escape Batman’s shadow. At the time, there was no other character quite like Oracle in comics. Barbara has extensive training in library sciences. This, when coupled with her world-class hacking skills, made her a true asset for the Bat Family and DC’s heroic community as a whole.

Recent findings suggest that and Barbara's actions in Breakout have driven home the notion that she does not need a heroic codename or a Batgirl outfit to be awesome. Barbara entered prison intending to help people, and while the cover to Breakout #10 casts doubt on whether she is successful, it is still a spectacular image, capturing everything great about the character. Even though the Batgirl suit is nowhere in sight, Gordon is still bringing the intensity.

Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10 is on sale February 10 from DC Comics!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

Industry observers note that writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Big Christmas Expansion.

According to recent reports, executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

According to recent reports, indieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”.

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

Industry observers note that “No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”.

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he stated, that was never really on his radar.

It has been revealed that “When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” said Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”.

The process was a “very challenging one,” he noted, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he noted. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really big influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”.

Sources indicate that he added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”.

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

Industry observers note that “In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he mentioned. But issues in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel stated of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.).

“Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he mentioned.).

Recent findings suggest that “When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”.

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in some ways, the best found-footage movie ever made is still The Blair Witch Project. This wasn’t because of the film’s actual quality, but because of the effect it had on audiences back in 1999. When it was released, found-footage movies just weren't a well-known thing and the marketing campaign for the movie made it seem as though the events depicted actually happened. Since then, better found-footage movies have been made that have replay value — a quality The Blair Witch Project sorely lacks — but none since have ever tricked audiences quite so effectively.

In a similar vein, Cloverfield, which is leaving Paramount Plus on Dec. 1, deserves its place in the found-footage movie hall of fame​​​​​​​, because Matt Reeves’ film remains a singular achievement nearly 20 years after its release, albeit for a very different reason.​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that cloverfield is about a group of young adults at a party in lower Manhattan when New York is invaded​​​​​​​ by a giant kaiju-like alien. At first, the friends are being escorted out of the city via the Brooklyn Bridge, but then Rob (Michael Stahl-David) gets a call from Beth (Odette Yustman), the woman he loves, who is part of the friend group​​​​​​​. Beth is trapped uptown in a half-collapsed building, so Rob resolves to save her and a few of his friends join him. Meanwhile, Hud (T.J. Miller), who was filming the party, keeps filming everything for posterity​​​​​​​.

In a recent development, now, Cloverfield didn’t trick people into believing it was real the way The Blair Witch Project did. After all, had New York City been destroyed by a giant monster, it would have at least been on the news. Still, Cloverfield did the next best thing by employing a truly mysterious marketing campaign.

According to recent reports, the very first trailer for Cloverfield merely highlighted the party going on. Then the partygoers saw a news report​​​​​​​ about something going on across town. Everyone hurries up to the roof of the building to get a better look and hear a huge roar​​​​​​​ in the distance. They see a giant explosion uptown with debris flying all over the city. Everyone rushes down to the street where another piece of debris lands nearby: the head of the Statue of Liberty​​​​​​​. The trailer ends there.

It has been revealed that as for the poster, it was merely a shot of Newly introduced York City beneath a cloud of smoke, with a headless Statue of Liberty looming over it​​​​​​​. You didn’t learn until you saw the movie that its plot centered on the giant alien terrorizing the city.​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that the movie also benefited from timing in a somewhat uncomfortable way. Released in 2008, just seven years after the terrorist attacks of Sep. 11, 2001, the film arrived while memories of the attacks were still fresh.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ With images of smoke-covered New York, collapsing buildings, and dust-filled city streets,​​​​​​​ the movie purposefully leaned into the real-life horrors of that day.

By 2008, there had already been a number of other found-footage films​​​​​​​ since The Blair Witch Project, but nothing like Cloverfield. Until then​​​​​​​, found-footage films​​​​​​​ weren't just an aesthetic choice, they were usually done out of financial necessity to make up for a slim budget. But Cloverfield was produced by J. J. Abrams and cost $30 million. By today’s standards, that’s not a huge budget for a movie, but it’s not an indie either.​​​​​​​ Cloverfield used the found-footage technique​​​​​​​ to take a unique approach to the giant-monster disaster genre​​​​​​​. Even today, found-footage movie​​​​​​​s are generally more grounded horror films that don’t really deal with monsters of that scale. Cloverfield is also different from other giant monster movies, because its found-footage approach creates an up-close, visceral experience that sets it apart.​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that and unlike something like The Blair Witch Project, Cloverfield does have replay value. It’s a solid monster movie with really great set pieces and characters you grow attached to. Even if you see things coming and you know which way the camera is going to swing next, the narrative is well-constructed and the creature is still really cool. That’s precisely why you should check out the movie one more time before it leaves Paramount Plus.​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that cloverfield is available to stream on Paramount Plus​​​​​​​ until Dec. 1.

#200311. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give.
  • With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful.
  • A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

According to recent reports, digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:.

It has been revealed that when time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

According to recent reports, include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”.

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:.

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

It has been revealed that spiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Industry observers note that mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

In a recent development, cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Industry observers note that sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Recent findings suggest that hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

Tech Report: The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Doubles Down On A Once Upon A Time In Hollywood Controversy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • Industry observers note that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself.
  • According to recent reports, that promptly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

Industry observers note that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself. After wowing audiences everywhere in 2019 with "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the quirky and uber-talented filmmaker returned to the scene of the crime (so to speak) once more with his long-awaited sequel/spin-off film, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." This time, the buddy comedy act with Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton and Brad Pitt's Cliff has been dropped, focusing solely on the latter as the stuntman embarks on his latest round of mischief. Though Tarantino stepped aside from his directing duties to make room for David Fincher, well, let's just say that the script is as purely QT as it gets.

According to recent reports, that promptly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before. You see, despite so much acclaim from critics and fans alike, "Once Upon a Time" drew the ire of many with its irreverent treatment of martial arts legend Bruce Lee, portrayed by Mike Moh in the film. Even Lee's family weighed in on the matter, objecting to how easily Cliff puts the arrogant Lee in his place during a fight scene on the set of a film. Not surprisingly, "Cliff Booth" returns to this fraught topic on several occasions, and it certainly feels like a meta-textual jab at the real-world backlash from before.

According to recent reports, was this in poor taste, or is Tarantino merely poking fun with a self-deprecating running joke? Moviegoers will undoubtedly have strong takes on either side. Here's where we land on our second go-around with this little debate.

You know, there's something to be mentioned for addressing an uncomfortable matter head-on instead of dancing around it — or even ignoring it altogether. Quentin Tarantino has never been one to shy away from a fight, a trait he happens to share with washed-up stuntman Cliff Booth. As a master cinephile, a brilliant bartender, a hit with the ladies, and a ruthless killer all in one, the power fantasy of it all isn't exactly hard to see in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Perhaps that's what made the Bruce Lee moment in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" stand out all the more (a fight that almost ended very differently). It's one thing for Cliff to be the coolest person alive in his world, and quite another for him to intrude rudely upon our own.

Sources indicate that so how does "Cliff Booth" address this elephant in the room? Although the incident is brought up on a number of occasions in passing, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II's buzzy actor Rodrick "Hot Rod" Harrison is positively fixated on it once he meets Cliff — a fact that also seems to catch the eye of talent manager Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). Intriguingly, Cliff himself almost seems embarrassed by the attention, perhaps self-reflexively brushing it off as the brash actions of a young man. Maybe, like Tarantino himself, he's a little older and a little wiser and less apt to repeat the same mistakes.

Industry observers note that less generously, the fact that this fight is emphasized so much in "Cliff Booth" could make the exact opposite point. It's treated almost like a legend or a myth in this world, giving Cliff a dangerous sense of aura and mystique that belies his charming appearance.

Either way, this is just one ingredient tossed into a much larger stew. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may struggle to reach the transcendent heights of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," but isn't that part of its point, too? "What is Cliff Booth without Rick Dalton?" Quentin Tarantino's script seems to be asking. Not dissimilarly, is a Tarantino movie with David Fincher at the wheel really a Tarantino movie anymore? Who can say how much ownership any of us have over our own art — or our lives in general?

Recent findings suggest that perhaps that's why "Cliff Booth" feels so much colder and mean-spirited than its predecessor. Although both films build to violent climaxes, the one in "Hollywood" is shot to be much more over-the-top and darkly funny than the one here. Before, Rick Dalton and Cliff were fighting to preserve a very specific way of life — one that the Manson family threatened to overturn. Here, Cliff very easily could've avoided the bloodshed with killers Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena), but he pursues this anyway out of ... ego? Principle? A sense of right and wrong? Cliff is a man of both simplicity and contradictions, so perhaps it's only fitting that the filmmaking style reflects this through Fincher's very different approach, as well.

That's where the repeated jabs about the Bruce Lee fight come in, as a moment that Cliff has no choice but to own. "Cliff Booth" is a movie about our attempts to define our own stories — whether it be himself, the troublemaking TV star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), or Karen. And maybe Bruce Lee, too.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in limited theaters.

The 10 Best Book Endings of All Time, Ranked

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you read a book, you're probably going to have to dedicate a whole bunch of time to it, unless it’s a novella or unless you're just a supernaturally fast reader.
  • Books don’t have to end amazingly to be great, since Frank Herbert honestly wasn’t very good at final chapters, but most of his Dune books are worth reading (most of them just sort of end abruptly, though to be fair, you can say the same about Jaws, and that’s a flawless movie regardless).
  • Industry observers note that novellas were mentioned before, and here’s one, technically: Animal Farm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you read a book, you're probably going to have to dedicate a whole bunch of time to it, unless it’s a novella or unless you're just a supernaturally fast reader. If you're in the latter camp, good on you. Also, lucky you. But hey, even if you're a fast reader, you're still going to want the destination to make the journey worth it. And if you're not a fast reader, then you're probably going to be even keener for the book you’ve spent a whole bunch of time on to end on a high note.

Books don’t have to end amazingly to be great, since Frank Herbert honestly wasn’t very good at final chapters, but most of his Dune books are worth reading (most of them just sort of end abruptly, though to be fair, you can say the same about Jaws, and that’s a flawless movie regardless). If you are after books with amazing endings, though, then the ones below are definitely worth checking out. If a book below ends surprisingly, then the fact the ending is surprising will be noted, but the specifics of the surprise won’t be. So, consider that a warning that there might be some mild spoilers (but nothing too in-your-face) below.

Industry observers note that novellas were mentioned before, and here’s one, technically: Animal Farm. Still, there’s a lot here packed into a relatively small number of pages, making Animal Farm more engaging and deep than a good many genuinely lengthy novels, because even if it’s technically about some animals on a farm (shock, horror) fighting for power, it’s actually about a whole lot more than that.

Or, more accurately, it’s about what you want it to be, depending on how you choose to break it down and all. In any event, the ending of Animal Farm packs a punch, even with it being the kind of thing that’s so iconic, it’s unlikely to count as a twist anymore. It happens, after so many years. It’s not quite the same as complaining about someone spoiling what happens by way of a massive natural disaster in the Book of Genesis (“Noah way,” people would say, if you could actually ruin it for them), but it’s also eventually not going to be too far off.

In a recent development, sometimes known as The Golden Compass, Northern Lights is the first book in the His Dark Materials trilogy, and because that whole trilogy ends a bit unusually, it probably has the strongest ending out of any of the books. That feels a little odd to say, yet it is its own book, and without it ending the way it does, it might not be as likely that you'd feel so invested and ready to tackle the next two books right after this one’s done.

Basically, Northern Lights has a good number of shocking moments for a young adult (or even children’s, according to some sources) novel, and there are reveals here that are honestly surprisingly bleak. It feels conclusive for a part one, all the while leaving a lot open for the rest of the series to explore, but in a thankfully genuinely satisfying manner.

Before you get to the ending, 11.22.63 is about an English teacher who’s given the chance to go back in time, but specifically to 1958. He views this as an opportunity to stay in the past for a while, until the titular date, when John F. Kennedy was assassinated, and on that date, he intends to prevent the assassination from happening, which seems like it’ll change the future for the better... that’s the proposal, at least.

And then the very end, without saying too much, does prove to be one of the most effortlessly emotional things Stephen King has ever written.

Much of 11.22.63 involves spending time to confirm who killed Kennedy while there, and then there are other forces that are harder to comprehend which seem to be working against him changing the past. When it gets to the end of things, though, it’s intense in a way that lives up to how suspenseful everything before the ending is, and then the very end, without saying too much, does prove to be one of the most effortlessly emotional things Stephen King has ever written in a very long (and mostly great) career.

In a recent development, brandon Sanderson has such a knack for concluding his books on high notes that there’s a term for the climaxes he tends to write: a Sanderlance. Basically, you're hit with a whole lot of drama packed into the final stretch of almost any given novel of his, and since some of his books are quite long, you're sometimes looking at 100+ pages of grand-scale action and surprising reveals, all in rapid succession.

You can feel a Brandon Sanderson book is a little slow-going at times, but then feel at ease that you're going to feel a sense of surprise (and, perhaps paradoxically, some unease) by the time you reach the last few chapters. Mistborn: The Final Empire might well have the most powerful Sanderlanche to date, and like with Northern Lights and its place within His Dark Materials, the way The Final Empire concludes is almost guaranteed to make you intrigued about how the next two Mistborn books might play out.

If Blood Meridian ever got made into a movie, it would ultimately be one of the most grueling and bloody of all time, even if it was just a fraction as violent as its source material. Also, Judge Holden would probably enter the ranks of the best monsters in cinema history, but as it stands, he has to settle for being one of the most memorable monstrous characters in literary history, since he is far and away the worst of a bad bunch.

It has been revealed that since it’s Cormac McCarthy being talked about, the notion that the Judge is one of the only people to emerge from Blood Meridian unscathed shouldn’t be too surprising, and it’s also the kind of book where you know it’s all going to end miserably about 10 or so pages in (or perhaps even earlier). Everything you’ve heard about this book and the ways it’s controversial are true, and while it is worth reading if you’ve got a strong enough stomach, definitely don’t read it if you're uncomfortable with a book that ends without even a hint of hope or anything approaching redemption for any of its characters.

Recent findings suggest that unpredictability is at play throughout the entirety of House of Leaves, which has the distinction of being incredibly intense for much of its duration while being, at some other points, honestly a little slow. There are things here that deliberately draw the novel as a whole out, and House of Leaves isn't afraid to slow down its pacing, and if you want to really get lost in some of the text that isn't strictly about the main part of the story, you can get distracted for a while. Thankfully, though, it does end up rewarding your time.

According to recent reports, the ending helps in that regard, even if there are still quite a few unanswered questions when all is stated and done, to say the least. There are a whole bunch of different narratives within House of Leaves (before even getting to how oddly the whole novel’s presented), so it’s not the kind of thing that wraps up neatly… though it does wrap up powerfully and memorably, admirably delivering more than just horror at the story’s end (even if horror is the genre ultimately explored most effectively in the bulk of House of Leaves).

Industry observers note that stoner is a book about a man living a life and that’s about it, but also, that’s everything, because that’s life. That could make Stoner something of a hard sell, but then again, at the same time, it’s hard to imagine too many people reading it and not getting anything out of it. The titular character grapples with the highs and lows of life, with more of an emphasis on the lows, and he overcomes a little but mostly just endures a whole lot.

Industry observers note that as a result, Stoner ends the way it always had to, because it’s a life story, beginning with the main character’s early stages of life and then ending when that life is no more. To say Stoner is ruinable would be like someone saying that learning they're going to die is a life spoiler. Finding meaning before that inevitable end is what's important, and that is what you get here (and it’s also what William Stoner thankfully finds, at least to some extent).

Industry observers note that before addressing or alluding to the ending, it has to be stressed that And Then There Were None has one of the best premises of all time, and then part of the reason it’s here is that the quality of the ending matches the quality of the premise. It’s immense all the way through, in other words, being perhaps the ultimate Agatha Christie novel, and one about ten people being told to go to an island and dying one by one.

According to recent reports, because they're all isolated, those who don’t die initially have to try to figure out who’s doing the murdering, and then, unsurprisingly, you, as a reader, are likely hooked. Of all the books here, it would feel like the biggest crime to ruin And Then There Were None, even with it being close to 90 years old, at the time of writing. It’s a fast-paced and relatively short book, too, so there’s little excuse not to read it, even if you're not exactly the biggest fan of reading in the world.

Recent findings suggest that like with The Stand and IT, which are some other classic (and lengthy) books by Stephen King, some people really don’t seem to like how The Dark Tower, as a series, concluded with the seventh main book, which was fittingly called The Dark Tower VII: The Dark Tower. It’s bold for sure, perhaps to a greater extent than even the ending found in IT, which might well be the only “more” controversial Stephen King ending in a career filled with somewhat divisive finales, but let it be known: these books have genuinely great endings.

There was a need to wrap up a lot here, and with The Dark Tower VII, Stephen King didn’t pull any punches, and then he also didn’t limit himself in terms of strange and offbeat ideas. There’s a sense of overwhelming finality here, alongside some admittedly anticlimactic (but in a purposeful way) elements, and then also a lot that’s surprisingly meta and introspective. It gives you a ton to think about and feel all at once, and it’s undoubtedly striking as a grand finale, proving difficult to forget and/or shake, for better or worse.

It has been revealed that whatever decade it had been published in, it’s inevitable that The Lord of the Rings would have been the top of that decade. It is just something special, so even if that’s a bit expected, and also maybe a bit boring to put it in the number one spot here, sorry, but it’s The Lord of the Rings. It has a bit of everything, including great characters, an immense world, a well-paced epic narrative, and a surprising amount of emotional weight.

It has been revealed that lots of the emotion comes at the end, expectedly, though by no means should The Lord of the Rings only be read for its ending (you'll realize sooner rather than later how good the journey is, almost regardless of the destination). There’s a whole lot of drama here, and a good many characters, but all the events and all those character arcs come to beyond-fitting conclusions by the time the whole epic novel wraps up (it’s a lengthy ending, especially if you read all those appendices, but undeniably worth it).

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. 10 Funniest Far Side Comics About Food
