📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Far Side made the ordinary seem strange and unpredictable.
  • According to recent reports, restaurants were a common location for The Far Side, and so were kitchen and dining room tables.
  • Sources indicate that below is a curated collection of the funniest uses of food in The Far Side, ranked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Far Side made the ordinary seem strange and unpredictable. It took elements from everyday life and remixed them to the oddball idiosyncratic tune that only creator Gary Larson danced to. Look at how he depicted food, for just one example.

According to recent reports, restaurants were a common location for The Far Side, and so were kitchen and dining room tables. Diner counters. School lunchrooms. And even barns where the cows were up to something they shouldn't be.

Sources indicate that below is a curated collection of the funniest uses of food in The Far Side, ranked. Disagree with the order here? Let us know what it should have been in the comments!

In a recent development, this Far Side cartoon came very early in Gary Larson's career, at a time when he was still figuring out his style. Both artistically and comedically. In retrospect, it almost feels like a joke a Far Side rip-off would make while trying to ape Larson's vibe.

In a recent development, in the cartoon, a waitress brings the "Prime Rib Papa" and "Viva la Vegetarian" dishes to a two-top, but refrains from assuming who ordered which dinner. The Neanderthal in an overcoat or the scientist. (Who, incidentally, stands out as a prototype for Futurama's Professor Farnsworth.) She doesn't want to judge a customer based on appearance, even if it seems super obvious.

In a recent development, "There's a fly in my soup!" It is a stock phrase, a joke that goes back a century. Perhaps even further than that. Often, the joke involves a patron at a restaurant making a fuss over it. In this Far Side cartoon, Gary Larson envisions a man discretely going to dispose of the insect instead, before he's stopped by the person eating next to him.

And by person, we mean frog. "I beg your pardon," a toad in a tiny fedora notes, before inquiring about the man's plans for the fly. In this way, it doubles as a take on another classic food-based punchline: "Are you going to eat that?".

According to recent reports, this Far Side joke is often cited among Gary Larson's best plays on words, and rightfully so. It is simple, but brilliant, and it fits into the "Goldilocks zone" of weird, dark humor. Not too weird, not too dark, but not too normal, or too light either. Here, "the crepes of wrath" strike, sticking in the throat of a man having breakfast at a café.

Consider the fact that a grape could also choke someone. Meaning this joke would have worked even if Larson hadn't touched the title of John Steinbeck's classic novel. Yet making it a crêpe instead is a memorable tweak that elevates the humor to a higher rung on the ladder of absurdity.

In a recent development, gary Larson loved to make jokes about mobsters. To the point where it was its own entire subgenre of Far Side joke. Which like most Far Side subgenres, got steadily weirder as Larson's career wore on. Peaking, in this case, with this "Sandwich Mafia" cartoon, where a sandwich snitch is thrown to the proverbial wolves, who are in this case literally ravenous fourth-graders.

Industry observers note that of all the different variations of this formula, this one is the most out there. Which makes it one of the best. And as revealing the ins-and-outs of how he came up with this sort of farcical Far Side masterpiece, no one was a stricter adherent to omerta than Larson.

"Mmmmm," one construction guy says to another, trying to really sell the fact that his sandwich tastes so good. So good that his co-worker might want to "trade for that banana" he brought in his lunch pail today. Plenty of people will know what this experience is like. What is askew in this scenario, in outrageous Far Side fashion, is what is between the bread.

That is, a skunk. It is a "skunk sandwich." Not only does that sound unappealing, it sounds utterly appalling. Baked into the premise of the joke is the fact that the guy knows it tastes terrible; that's why he's trying to trade. The greater, more absurd gag, though, is the unanswerable question of why he has a skunk sandwich in the first place.

Industry observers note that "That...is not how you do it at all." Ever see someone doing something so wrong that you're just left speechless? That's what this Far Side cartoon is going for. Just a jaw-dropping level of ineptitude. Yet, improbably, it still gets the job done.

At this diner, ordering flapjacks is an ordeal. Because the chef doesn't use a spatula to flip the pancake. He picks up the entire stove and jerks it upward, sending the golden brown disc up into the air. Still, give him credit. His method is unorthodox, and his spelling is terrible, but he clearly gets the job done.

Gary Larson was a master of language. That's obvious in The Far Side's best (and/or worst) puns, but it is also apparent more latently in plenty of other Far Side jokes. Like this one, where Larson pokes fun at peoples' tendencies to personify body parts and organs, the stomach in particular.

It isn't Gordon that is breaking his diet late at night, it is "his own stomach." Which Larson brilliantly visualizes with an illustration of a disembodied stomach standing in front of an open refrigerator. If only Gordon could keep his stomach under control, he'd live a very different life.

One of Gary Larson's most infamous cartoons. A pseudo-sequel to a Far Side joke where a cow named "Jesse" is caught grilling up some steaks and is called out for being "sick," in this panel a bunch of bovines have become curious to learn what all the fuss is about with their meat.

So, they gather around as one of them taste tests a T-bone, hilariously (and darkly) declaring that it "taste[s] a little like chicken." It is the perfect example of a Far Side cartoon where the familiar becomes twisted, and the twisted becomes absurd, and the absurd becomes laugh-out-loud funny.

Recent findings suggest that released six years earlier, this Far Side panel is spiritually similar to the previous one. It is about making dinner into an unexpectedly dark scene. This is also an all-time great example of Gary Larson's fondness for messing with nursery rhymes, as well as a subversive bit of Far Side wordplay.

"Mary Has a Little Lamb" becomes Mary had "a little lamb" for dinner, with "three helpings of corn, two baked potatoes, [and] extra bread." She does this "with her blinds pulled," hilariously suggesting she knows how shocking it is that her pet lamb has become her supper.

According to recent reports, this is the best Far Side food joke, there's little room for doubt. Captioned 'when potato salad goes bad," it features a man opening his fridge to find the salad pointing a gun at some innocent bystanding condiments. What makes this so perfect is that it replicates the experience of reading The Far Side, especially when it was first being published.

Open up the newspaper and find something you didn't expect to see that day. Something surreal and ridiculous. "When potato salad goes bad" is a pun, but it is also a literal scenario in a world operating by its own Larsonian dream logic. It is one of the best Far Side jokes period, because of how effortlessly funny it is while still being something few people besides Gary Larson would come up with.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that being the third sequel to "Meet the Parents," this week's "Focker In-Law" (you can read our review here) has a lot on its plate. Its intention is to act as a direct follow-up to 2010's "Little Fockers," yet it also aims to lightly reset the franchise's premise and, unlike most other legacy sequels, retain a tight focus on the property's original lead, Greg Focker (Ben Stiller), and his neurotic shenanigans. On the whole, then, writer/director John Hamburg has his hands full with all that plus balancing a rather large ensemble of actors, ranging from returning players like Stiller, Robert De Niro, and Owen Wilson to newcomers such as Ariana Grande. Basically, the film doesn't really have the time to incorporate a bunch of cheeky nods to its stars' past work.

This is why it's even more delightful to see a little tribute to one of Stiller's other popular comedies snuck into the body of "Focker In-Law." Rather than Stiller or the like awkwardly making a verbal reference, the tribute is elegantly woven into a couple of the film's gags. Indeed, one of the tenets of the "Meet the Parents/Fockers" franchise is that Greg needs to be put through the ringer both emotionally and physically, and Hamburg finds multiple ways to accomplish this throughout "Focker In-Law." Near the beginning of the movie, for instance, Greg is accidentally burned in the face, while later, he's nearly frozen to death. In addition to these jokes being part of the movie piling misery onto Greg, they double as a sly nod to Stiller's transgressive action comedy flick "Tropic Thunder," in which his character similarly endured extreme temperatures. It's subtle enough to be missed yet clever enough to stand out.

2008's "Tropic Thunder" begins with some table-setting in-universe movie trailers for other fictional films starring the actors who, in the body of the film, are making a Vietnam war movie. One of these is for a film starring Tugg Speedman (Ben Stiller), and it's the latest in his "Scorcher" franchise. But where the prior "Scorcher" movies have starred Speedman as a hero saving a baby in the middle of a fiery apocalypse, "Scorcher VI: Global Meltdown" sees Speedman's hero return after an eclipse plunges the post-apocalyptic Earth into freezing temperatures. (Also, he's now looking after two babies instead of just one.).

It has been revealed that by comparison, in "Focker In-Law," Greg wants to cook his father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) his favorite meal, but his son's fresh girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande), wants to use the kitchen to make an alternate meal for Jack at the same time. So, Greg and Olivia, having already gotten off on the wrong foot, compete while cooking, which naturally results in Greg becoming careless and nearly burning his own face off, leaving him with a scorched appearance for a while. From there, he goes on to meet up with Jack, who's now all into health and wellness and insists that the pair talk during a cold plunge, which Greg assures him he's done before. But he hasn't, of course, and he ends up not being able to take the extreme cold.

Industry observers note that with these two moments combined, Stiller is once again put in the middle of both extreme heat and extreme cold. However, in stark contrast to Tugg Speedman, Greg can't handle either temperature. It's a cute way of acknowledging Stiller's on-screen past while once again dunking pretty mercilessly on Greg.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

Sources indicate that during the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More.

It has been revealed that “To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”.

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”.

More coverage from our Craft Roundtables can be found here.

It has been revealed that it's been eight years since Josh Brolin last played CIA operative Matt Graver in Sicario: Day of the Soldado, and while there's been talk of a third movie for much of that time, Brolin has since reunited with Sicario director Denis Villeneuve for his adaptation of Dune. Brolin's career has taken him from the American frontier in True Grit to the deserts of Arrakis in the Dune films, but his latest project has more in common with one of HBO's greatest television series, Band of Brothers, and he'll be helping Netflix tell the story of the men whose experiences inspired that series.

According to recent reports, brolin's new documentary series, World War II: Behind Enemy Lines, will officially premiere on Netflix on December 2, with all four episodes available to stream in just five days. The series tells the story of the 101st Airborne's battles, covert missions, and losses in Nazi-occupied Europe, starting with the D-Day landings in June 1944 and ending with V-E Day in May 1945. Think of it as the real-life version of the story many people know from Band of Brothers.

Similar to the work done by Peter Jackson in bringing World War I footage to color and 3D, this is built from archive film that's been restored to the highest quality and colorized too, while much of it is previously unseen and includes rare first-hand accounts from the men who were there. And in a rare, fascinating move, it also shows the German paratroopers who were defending Normandy before the sea landings.

Recent findings suggest that the series comes from 72 Films, the production company behind Netflix's six-part documentary World War II: From the Frontlines, which was narrated by John Boyega (Star Wars: The Force Awakens) and went on to win two Emmy Awards in 2024. Director Rob Coldstream is back for the upcoming series, with David Glover and Mark Raphael serving as executive producers and Brolin taking over narration duties.

While From the Frontlines covered the war across multiple countries and from the perspectives of those on opposing sides, the fresh series will focus specifically on the experiences of the American soldiers who served with the 101st Airborne Division in Europe.

World War II: Behind Enemy Lines premieres on Netflix on December 2. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and highlights heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A futuristic noir setting indebted to a mish-mash of Japanese aesthetics and populated by off-putting robots, all wrapped up in an existentialist nightmare ruled by soulless corporations?
  • So, when it came to following both Scott's film and Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," "Blade Runner 2099" showrunner Silka Luisa opted to let the series' freak flag fly in the best way imaginable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, of all the movies to turn into a franchise, "Blade Runner" might be the unlikeliest of them all. Much of that stems from Ridley Scott's 1982 original, famously a flop upon release, arriving well ahead of its time and forcing audiences to catch up to its very specific vision of post-apocalyptic Los Angeles. But there's also the much more obvious factor that prevented this from reaching true blockbuster heights: It's just so damn weird.

A futuristic noir setting indebted to a mish-mash of Japanese aesthetics and populated by off-putting robots, all wrapped up in an existentialist nightmare ruled by soulless corporations? It's admittedly a hard sell for most mainstream audiences — or perhaps one that simply hits a little too close to home. But that's also what makes this such a vast and endlessly fascinating world to explore.

So, when it came to following both Scott's film and Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," "Blade Runner 2099" showrunner Silka Luisa opted to let the series' freak flag fly in the best way imaginable. During a recent press junket, I spoke with the writer over Zoom to ask about pushing the envelope and making things as weird as possible. As it turns out, this approach is perfectly embodied by secondary antagonist and unruly Replicant Clotilde, played by Amy Lennox, and her silly-looking hat:.

"One thing that [director Jonathan van Tulleken], who did episodes 1 and 2, was so good about — we were like partners in crime. For example, Amy has a crazy Moebius hat on in Episode 2 when you first meet her [...] But I remember on the day, I was like, 'Jay, I don't know if we should do the hat.' And he was like, 'The hat's amazing. We're doing the hat. We have to do the hat.' [Laughs]".

Although the character has remained out of sight and mind throughout the marketing of "Blade Runner 2099," Clotilde will rapidly win viewers over as one of the more vibrant and unpredictable characters of Season 1. Inevitably, she stands out all the more in a show otherwise defined by the idea of conformity — something that holds life-or-death stakes for Hunter Schafer's Cora, a human posing as a Replicant Blade Runner for the LAPD. Yet, on the other end of the spectrum, Clotilde's Replicant antagonist comes with an outsized personality ... and an over-the-top costume to match.

Sources indicate that according to Silka Luisa, this ended up becoming a nice bit of shorthand for their ongoing mandate, both during filming and as they put the season together. "It was like that, but with everything: Always go for the hat." For the showrunner, however, pushing themselves to go bigger and weirder had even broader applications. In fact, its roots go all the way back to Philip K. Dick, the author of the novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and the source material for "Blade Runner" as a whole. (Here's what Dick thought of Ridley Scott's original movie.) As Luisa explains, a little bit of levity can go a long way in a world as bleak as this:.

According to recent reports, "But that is so P. K. Dick. When you read his book, he has really dark ideas about what our future will be, what technology is going to do to us. And you need the hat. Because when you don't have it, it's too hard to exist in those conversations for very long.".

"Blade Runner 2099," hat and all, is now streaming on Prime Video.

Latest Update: ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs.
  • It has been revealed that while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients.
  • In a recent development, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her new friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

It has been revealed that while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy.

In a recent development, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

Sources indicate that “In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” noted Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”.

Industry observers note that the scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her new companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

“I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” noted Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”.

Industry observers note that hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

Industry observers note that “The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very important and really supports this scene,” stated Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”.

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

“I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”.

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”.

According to recent reports, “There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

Industry observers note that “For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very key turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”.

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

While details about the upcoming movie remain limited, Amazon is reportedly targeting a 2028 release. With a fresh era of Bond on the horizon, now might be a good time to revisit the franchise's previous adventures. Just don't wait until December to do it on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app.
  • It has been revealed that to use Task, open Gemini and create a latest chat.
  • Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

It has been revealed that to use Task, open Gemini and create a latest chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Recent findings suggest that gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

Industry observers note that while Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro customers. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is presently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

In a recent development, some features, though, are only for U.S. people. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Sources indicate that gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any important steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free initiative, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes.
  • So far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding fresh stars to the Focker family and beyond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains minor spoilers for "Focker In-Law.".

It has been revealed that although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes. After all, while most of the great comedy sequels earn their status by being just as much or nearly as unique as their predecessors, if the jokes are lacking, then it's all for naught. This is why many comedy sequels are identified not by their character arcs or plot but by their gags and setpieces. "Gremlins 2: The New Batch" will primarily be known for its inclusion of wilder and weirder Gremlins, "Addams Family Values" has a memorable Thanksgiving play sequence, and so on.

So far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding fresh stars to the Focker family and beyond. "Meet the Fockers" introduced Barbara Streisand and Dustin Hoffman as the parents of Ben Stiller's Greg Focker, while "Little Fockers" used the occasion of the Fockers having babies to include new faces such as Jessica Alba's Andi. This month's "Focker In-Law" continues the tradition by casting hot young talents Skyler Gisondo and Beanie Feldstein as the Focker children, with Ariana Grande also turning up in a major role as Greg's son's fiancé. However, writer/director John Hamburg cleverly understood that he couldn't solely rely on the cast to make his film stand out. He wanted to conceive a sequence that would match the cringe comedy outrageousness of the original film while using all his stars in a major way. He does so in the moment where Greg sings John Legend's "All of Me" to Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), which, according to Hamburg himself, is the best scene in the movie.

One of the things "Focker In-Law" does really well is escalation, in which Greg Focker makes a series of choices which have minor consequences at first but promptly snowball into increasingly more ludicrous events. The apex of this is when Greg (Ben Stiller), who has taken it upon himself to keep Henry (Skyler Gisondo) from proposing to Olivia (Ariana Grande) by hiding the engagement ring, discovers at the last minute that Henry had secretly planned to sing a song at dinner with everyone present. Scrambling, Greg decides to perform the song himself, and dedicate it to his occasional family nemesis, Jack.

In a recent development, when I had the opportunity to speak to Hamburg about the movie, he chose this setpiece as the best scene in the film from a subjective and objective perspective. As he explained:.

"I'd say for this movie, it's recency bias, but there's a scene where Greg serenades Jack. And most of the cast is sitting around this table and Owen Wilson's at the piano. And that was just a really epic moment in my career as a filmmaker. To have these amazingly talented people gathered on one set and then have Ben singing and Bob's reactions are so priceless. It was just like everything kind of came together. That's like the dream for a comedy filmmaker, to have that. And then the audience reaction was so great. [...] There's many [great scenes], but of many, I'd say that sequence is one I reflect on. It's like, that was a really fun couple of days of shooting.".

Given how well it works both in and out of context, the scene is absolutely a standout moment. And who knows, maybe Stiller will sing again in the next "Focker" film because of it.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and substantial mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game.

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”.

According to recent reports, the cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover upcoming series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three latest series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

Deadline first reported the news.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals. He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms. His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of Newly introduced York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director. In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

Recent findings suggest that ask 10 true cinephiles for the best crime movie of the 2000s, and you will likely get 10 different answers. It's what makes this particular topic so fascinating to argue about. There is a smorgasbord of intensely dramatic genre-related crime films that most other decades cannot match. Directors who had spent the 1990s learning the genre suddenly had the budgets and the freedom to push those conventions into even further realms. This is a highly thought of list, critically speaking, with three of the entries appearing on The Upcoming York Times list of the 100 best movies of the 21st century.

Sources indicate that several of these films have returned to the pop culture conversation. The Departed turned 20 on October 6th, and returns to U.S. theaters on December 4th for a limited anniversary run. Memento turned 25 in March, with a newly introduced 4K Blu-ray with a Dolby Vision master that comes Christopher Nolan approved. Catch Me If You Can has bounced between Paramount+, Hulu and Pluto TV this year. If you want a weekend marathon for the holiday, most of these are easy to find. Streaming rights switch constantly, so check before you go to queue up.

Recent findings suggest that A few notes on how this list works. I leaned on rewatchability, critical response, and cultural influence. It means that a few louder box office hits land lower than some might expect. Two of the movies are directorial debuts, which say something about the health of the genre during the decade. Spoilers stay light, though the entries mention a few pivotal moments.

Gone Baby Gone was Ben Affleck's debut as a director and may be one of the lesser known movies in this list. The narrative unfolds with a missing child, and rapidly dissolves into a story about how far people will go to fix a mistake. Casey Affleck plays Patrick Kenzie, a young private investigator in Dorchester, with a boyish look that hides a stubborn moral streak. Michelle Monaghan is Angie Gennaro, his partner and girlfriend. She gets some of the sharpest scenes, and is key in helping with the search for four-year-old Amanda McCready. The ending turns on a decision that splits viewers and becomes quite the moral puzzle in its final stretch.

According to recent reports, ben Affleck co-wrote the script with Aaron Stockhard from a Dennis Lehane novel. Amy Madigan and Titus Welliver play the girl's aunt and uncle. Morgan Freeman is the police captain in charge of the case, and Ed Harris appears as a hard-edged detective. Amy Ryan earned an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress, and Affleck later went on to direct The Town and then Argo, which won Best Picture. This was certainly a very promising first step, a project that landed a 94% RT critics score and an 86% audience score. The movie runs just under two hours, and it has been streaming on Paramount+ all year.

Recent findings suggest that christopher Nolan's second feature stars Guy Pearce and opens with a Polaroid fading back into a camera. Nolan keeps the reversals coming from there, as the audience learns about Leonard Shelby (Pearce), a man with anterograde amnesia. He cannot form upcoming memories after an attack that killed his wife. Leonard tracks her killer using Polaroids, notes and tattoos on his body. Carrie-Anne Moss and Joe Pantoliano play the people who may or may not be helping him.

Recent findings suggest that memento premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2000. Early on several distributors reportedly passed because they worried audiences could not follow the structure. The narrative structure is culturally known for moving backwards in color and forward in black and white. Nolan adapted the movie from a short story by his brother Jonathan called Memento Mori. The DVD included a menu puzzle that viewers had to solve to watch the story in chronological order. It added to its cult status, along with the multiple Oscar nominations.

Daniel Craig is credited only as XXXX in Layer Cake, Matthew Vaughn's first film as a director. He had previously produced two Guy Ritchie movies, and directs here from J.J. Connolly's adaptation of his own novel. XXXX is a cocaine dealer who treats crime as a day job. He looks to retire, but his boss hands him two tasks to complete. Of course, neither went as he had planned. One is finding a missing young woman, and the other is brokering a massive London drug deal. Michael Gambon, Colm Meaney, Siena Miller, and a young Tom Hardy round out the ensemble cast.

Craig's calm and tailored performance reportedly caught the eye of Bond's producers, and he was cast as 007 in 2005. Metacritic scores Layer Cake at 73. Vaughn's debut project operates like a British gangster story that treats the job like an office with bosses, middlemen, and deliberately bad communication. Vaughn would later go on to direct Kick-Ass, X Men: First Class and Kingsman.

The Departed is a Boston remake of the 2002 Hong Kong thriller, Infernal Affairs. Martin Scorsese directs, and Leonardo DiCaprio is Billy Costigan, a young state trooper sent undercover into the crew of Jack Nicholson's Frank Costello. The premise is built on the clever idea that a cop and criminal's worlds are much closer than one might expect. Matt Damon plays Colin Sullivan, a criminal who has risen inside the State Police as Costello's mole. Nicholson plays the gangster with his usual gusto, and Martin Sheen and Mark Wahlberg provide the police side of things.

Sources indicate that vera Farmiga plays a psychiatrist caught between both men. Scorsese hides X marks in the frame before characters die, a nod to the 1932 Scarface. The Departed won four Oscars, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Film Editing. Wahlberg netted a Best Supporting Actor nomination, and the movie grossed about $291 million worldwide. It turned 20 this year, and returns to the big screen for a limited theatrical run starting December 4th.

Recent findings suggest that antoine Fuqua directed Training Day from a script by David Ayer. The story unfolds over a single day in the LAPD's narcotics unit. Ethan Hawke plays rookie Jake Hoyt, an eager officer on his first day with Denzel Washington's Alonzo Harris, a veteran detective who breaks every rule imaginable. The supporting cast includes Scott Glenn, Tom Berenger, Eva Mendes, Dr. Dre, and Snoop Dogg. Washington, known for playing heroes, plays Alonzo with a grin that keeps the audience off balance.

The suspense is drawn from watching Jake try to figure out where the lessons end and the crimes begin. It makes it so the audience and Jake can never truly relax. Washington won the Oscar for Best Actor at the 2002 ceremony, and Hawke saw a Best Supporting Actor nomination. Fuqua's career took off after Training Day, and gave Ayer a platform for the cop stories he would write later. Ayer went on to make Harsh Times and End of Watch, and Training Day turned 25 in October. The final stretch pulls Jake into a confrontation with Alonzo that Washington sells with sheer intensity. Alonzo remains one of the most quoted villains of the 2000s.

Industry observers note that catch Me If You Can opens with stylish animated credits that set the 1960s tone before Leonardo DiCaprio even shows up. The narrative focuses on DiCaprio's Frank Abagnale Jr., a teenage con man who poses as an airline pilot, a doctor, and a lawyer all while forging millions of dollars in checks. DiCaprio plays Frank with his early career boyish charm, and Tom Hanks is Carl Hanratty, the FBI agent who chases him across the country with growing admiration.

In a recent development, john Williams wrote a fantastic jazzy score, and Christopher Walken is Frank's father who yearns to be proud of his son. Both earned Oscar nominations for their contributions. Martin Sheen, Amy Adams, and Nathalie Baye appear in smaller roles. The movie grossed more than $352 million worldwide on a $52 million budget and sits at 96% on RT. Spielberg released Minority Report earlier the same year, which makes 2002 one of his busiest and brightest years. Hanratty's Christmas Eve phone call with Frank is one of the movie's most memorable scenes.

Recent findings suggest that zodiac is a crime movie about people who cannot let go. The story follows the hunt for the Zodiac Killer, who terrorized the San Francisco Bay Area in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Jake Gyllenhaal plays obsessive cartoonist Robert Graysmith, Mark Ruffalo is inspector Dave Toschi, and Robert Downey Jr. plays reporter Paul Avery, whose life unravels as the case drags on. Anthony Edwards, Brian Cox and Chloë Sevigny fill out the supporting cast. David Fincher directs from James Vanderbilt's script, based on Graysmith's books.

Fincher stages the killer's attacks with a cold realism, including the Lake Berryessa scene and the cab murder in San Francisco. A late sequence in a basement may be the most frightening scene in the movie, even though almost nothing happens. Zodiac did modestly at the box office, but it has since grown massively in critical and commercial reputation. The case never reaches a clear answer, much like the reality of it all, yet the attention to period piece detail and the frustration surrounding the mystery fuels the narrative engine.

Recent findings suggest that no Country for Old Men feels like a western that wandered into a nightmare. Joel and Ethan Coen adapted Cormac McCarthy's novel into a bleak, darkly funny crime story set in West Texas in 1980. Josh Brolin is Llewelyn Moss, a welder who finds drug money in the desert, and Javier Bardem plays Anton Chigurh, a hitman with a pageboy haircut and a captive bolt pistol. The epic won four Oscars, including Best Picture, Best Director for the Coens, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Supporting Actor for Bardem.

Industry observers note that roger Deakins shoots the project with a stark clarity. Tommy Lee Jones plays Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, who opens the movie with a weary narration about the passing of time and the increase in violence in the modern world. Woody Harrelson and Kelly Macdonald add key supporting roles and Carter Burwell's score is so sparse that the silence does much of the work. The gas station coin toss scene is a masterclass in tension built simply out of dialogue and RT lists the western at 93%. The ending still divides viewers, which keeps people arguing about it to this day.

It has been revealed that christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight turns Gotham into a crime city and Batman into a detective in a bodysuit. The sequel to Batman Begins opens with a bank robbery that sets the tone for everything that follows. Christian Bale returns as Bruce Wayne, Aaron Eckhart is district attorney Harvey Dent, and Gary Oldman is Commissioner Jim Gordon. Heath Ledger's Joker plans the heist, and he disposes of his crew in a manner that foreshadows to the audience, the societal collapse he hopes to execute. Maggie Gyllenhaal, Michael Caine, and Morgan Freeman complete the main cast.

Nolan shot key action sequences with IMAX cameras and filmed in Chicago, which gives the city its scale. Ledger passed away in January 2008, six months before release, and he won a posthumous Oscar for Best Supporting Actor. The Dark Knight grossed more than $1 billion worldwide and appears on the Latest York Times list of the best movies of the 21st century. Nolan has cited Michael Mann's Heat as an influence, which explains why Gotham feels like a crime city with a manic sociopathic clown in the middle. The interrogation scene between Batman and the Joker is the centerpiece and still is quoted to this day.

  • In a recent development, earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen? Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out.

Recent findings suggest that at the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In a recent development, in Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

It has been revealed that there are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

Recent findings suggest that there are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

Latest Update: 5 Best Book Series To Read If You Like The Hunger Games

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem. When Katniss' beloved younger sister Primrose is chosen, or "reaped," via a random lottery to participate in the annual Games (where two "tributes" from all 12 districts are forced to compete to the death on live television until one victor emerges), Katniss volunteers as tribute, and her time as a Hunger Games participant begins.

Sources indicate that "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010. Naturally, a "Hunger Games" film franchise followed in 2012 and spawned four blockbusters. ("Mockingjay" got split into two parts, something that director Francis Lawrence regrets.) Then, in 2020, Collins released her first literary "Hunger Games" prequel, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — which centers on the origin story of future Panem president Coriolanus Snow — and five years later, we got "Sunrise on the Reaping," which explains precisely how Katniss' eventual friend and mentor (and her fellow District 12 victor) Haymitch Abernathy won his Games.

If you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next? From dystopian classics to other YA favorites, we've got some ideas.

A lot of dystopian novels are referred to as "speculative fiction," which means that the scenario laid out by the author could conceivably happen in real life ... so, let's hope that Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah's novel "Chain-Gang All-Stars" doesn't come to pass. Released in 2023, this novel imagines a world where the incarceration system in the United States is, somehow, even worse than it is in our reality — in that prisoners are allowed to enroll in a program called CAPE, which stands for "Criminal Action Penal Entertainment." Not only are the inmates in CAPE constantly monitored (with their every move broadcast to hungry audiences), they're also sent across the country to constantly participate in gladiator matches against each other that are, you guessed it, televised as well. The book's title comes from the reimagined version of a traditional "chain gang," where the prisoner-gladiators are called "Links" and given two options to leave: either they're High Freed, meaning released, or Low Freed, meaning killed.

Throughout "Chain-Gang All-Stars," we follow the Angola-Hammond Chain in the system and, more specifically, Hamara "Hurricane Staxxx" Stacker and Loretta "Blood Mama" Thurwar, the two female fighters in a secret relationship who open the book. As we move through the unsettling world Adjei-Brenyah concocted in "Chain-Gang All Stars," we follow a wide variety of prisoners participating in this gut-wrenching game ... and it's sort of impossible to not think of the "Hunger Games" franchise as you read it, albeit in a good way. After you wrap up all five "Hunger Games" books, check out "Chain-Gang All-Stars." (Nina Starner).

In a recent development, when it comes to seeing people die horrible deaths in death games televised for the entertainment of an oppressive ruling class, no book does it on a larger scale than Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl." The book takes place after Earth has been taken over by an alien corporation that seeks to mine the planet for resources. Those who aren't killed during the initial invasion are then forced to compete in an intergalactic reality show program, an RPG-like "dungeon crawl" where they have to navigate various levels of a labyrinthian dungeon, each filled with increasingly dangerous monsters and scenarios.

What makes "Dungeon Crawler Carl" unique is how it blends together ridiculous video game and tabletop RPG logic with an unhealthy dose of pop culture references, the humor of a Douglas Adams book, and the brutality and social commentary about unchecked capitalism and authoritarianism of "The Hunger Games." Indeed, reading Dinniman's book and its follow-ups is like playing a fun RPG session, in that it's chaotic, messy, hilarious, and weird, all while packing a serious emotional punch full of heartbreak and cruel twists and turns. But rather than reveling in their misery, Dinniman's characters rage against the corporate machine in an effort to break it. What you end up with is a story about the necessity of resistance and the importance of community, both of which are themes that will resonate with "Hunger Games" fans. And did I mention it features an endlessly quotable talking cat? (Rafael Motamayor).

I don't think it's possible to have a conversation about young adult dystopian books and films like the "Hunger Games" stories without discussing "The Handmaid's Tale." Margaret Atwood's landmark 1980 book set a standard for dystopian narratives rivaled only by George Orwell's "1984," but Atwood's specificity is what makes her imagined world so terrifying — in that "The Handmaid's Tale" takes place in a world where a religious totalitarian regime oppresses women and queer people. Offred (meaning "of Fred"), our heroine, works as one of the titular handmaids, which means she's prized for her fertility and used as a "vessel" (that's putting it politely) for her Commander, Fred, to impregnate instead of his un-fertile wife. As Offred exists in Gilead (which forbids women from having quite literally any rights and punishes them with death if they even try to stray), we follow her every move in the novel, learning bits and pieces about her life before Gilead as June, a mother and wife with the freedom to live as she pleased.

"The Handmaid's Tale" was adapted into a Hulu series in 2017, and while I do think Elisabeth Moss did an incredible job playing Offred, the show ran through Atwood's book by the end of Season 1 and kept its wheels spinning for, in my opinion, far too long (although it at least gets its final message right.) If you haven't read Atwood's book but are familiar with its well-known red costumes and overall vibe, I couldn't possibly recommend it more. Its prose is beautiful, its subject matter is terrifying, and it's a clear precursor to and inspiration for the stories found in the "Hunger Games" franchise. (Nina Starner).

Though certainly not as dark in tone as "The Hunger Games," the pop culture celebration that is author Ernest Cline's "Ready Player One" is an oddly fitting companion piece for fans of the world Suzanne Collins built. One could even look at it as a bit of a palette cleanser, albeit one that still scratches a similar itch.

For those not familiar, the book takes place in 2044 and focuses on Wade Watts, who spends his days in the virtual utopia known as the OASIS. Wade's devoted his life to studying the puzzles hidden within this world's digital confines, themselves based on their creator's fixation on pop culture — with the promise of massive power and fortune to whoever can unlock them.

Industry observers note that "Ready Player One" is jam-packed with pop culture references and is lighthearted in a lot of ways. However, it's also terribly dystopian, as the OASIS is not only people's sole escape from the harsh realities of the outside world, there's very little person-to-person communication anymore outside of the virtual space. Beyond that, the rush to solve the puzzles and nab the fortune results in a deadly game for Wade and many others, which is where the "Hunger Games" of it all comes in.

Industry observers note that steven Spielberg's 2018 movie adaptation left a lot to be desired for many fans and, yes, a "Ready Player Two" movie was in the works in 2021, though it's yet to materialize. Setting the film aside, the novel remains a true gem filled with wonderful world building, fully-realized characters, and just a dash of "kill or be killed" to make the whole thing extra exciting, elevating it beyond the barrage of references it might have otherwise been. (Ryan Scott).

The funny thing about Pierce Brown's "Red Rising" series is that the first book in the still-ongoing saga is very much a "Hunger Games" riff ... until it's not. Set in a distant future where humanity has been rigidly split into various genetically modified castes that determine a person's role in society, the story follows Darrow, a young Martian "red" whose wife is murdered by the ruling "gold" regime, sending him on a quest for revenge that ultimately spans the entire solar system. But before the sweeping space opera can begin, Darrow infiltrates the gold caste and must survive the Institute, a deadly school where young people are violently set against one another in not-so-simulated combat and conquest.

Those who enjoyed the blend of youthful angst, action, sci-fi world-building, and dystopian politics of "The Hunger Games" will take quickly and easily to "Red Rising," which offers a similar flavor with a harsher, more masculine edge. However, starting with the second book "Golden Son" and continuing into later installments, Brown takes things in a wholly new direction, turning his Suzanne Collins riff into the kind of sprawling, detailed, intense, and morally murky epic that would make Frank Herbert and George R.R. Martin proud. This is the perfect stepping stone for "Hunger Games" fans hoping to branch out into a different flavor of science fiction. It's familiar enough, until it is suddenly, and brutally, not. (Jacob Hall).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is getting an audience ovation.

Seven years ago, Quentin Tarantino introduced his fictionalized Hollywood world around the time of the Tate murders with Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. One of the standout roles was Rick Dalton's (Leonardo DiCaprio) stuntman Cliff Booth, and Brad Pitt's portrayal won him an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. Now, he's elevated to the leading star in his own sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, with David Fincher taking over as director. Before it lands on Netflix next month, however, the movie has already made its way to IMAX theaters for its two-week exclusive run.

Recent findings suggest that with over 100 verified ratings, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth debuts to a solid 88% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Surprisingly, that's 18 points higher than Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, which had 70%. Meanwhile, it's the third-highest-rated project between Fincher and Pitt, who reunite for the fourth time after Fight Club (96%), Se7en (95%), and The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (80%).

Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019).

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026).

The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008).

Reviews of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth praised Pitt's charming return as the titular character, while the movie is powered by its supporting cast, including Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, and Peter Weller. However, the more intriguing assessment was the blend of Fincher's sleek directorial flair with Tarantino's signature dialogue. Although the filmmakers couldn't be more different in style, critics couldn't agree more that the team-up works. Furthermore, with the sequel set eight years after the original, critics praised its 1970s atmosphere and production design.

According to recent reports, however, not everything about the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel turned out flawless. Some reviewers noted that the narrative structure was thin, with the story feeling more episodic than tightly driven.

While many moviegoers also enjoyed the sequel, the high audience score is surprising given some of the controversy. Just ahead of its release, Fincher confirmed that AI was used in the movie. As a result, some viewers are looking back retrospectively at certain visual anomalies, sparking discussion on where the tool was applied.

Industry observers note that fincher defended his decision, saying: "It was all done to enhance the work of “real human beings." Additionally, he elaborated that it was used to clean up areas like background audio: "That's all AI. We used AI to clean up those tracks.".

Despite the backlash, the Cliff Booth sequel still seems to be doing well with viewers, with an audience score higher than Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, which also wasn't without controversy over the altered historical change to the Tate murders and the depiction of Bruce Lee. Meanwhile, the box office projections in the coming days will indicate its commercial performance, albeit limited since it's only for IMAX. The original 2019 movie made $410 million against a $90–96 million budget.

The Further Mis-Aventures of Cliff Booth is now playing in IMAX before it goes to Netflix on December 23.
